The framework describes the interpreter who continues to explain after correction is needed, or the defender who cannot acknowledge a legitimate revision. Audience rewards can reinforce repeated performance, but observed persistence does not establish an inner compulsion. Identify the original function, the changed conditions, the continued behavior, and the practical cost. A person may change roles across episodes; the goal is to restore flexibility rather than classify them permanently. The appropriate response may be to invite correction, transfer responsibility, or stop rewarding the obsolete performance.
#### Family 03.04.E — Launch Fields, First Contact and Circulation Paths

This family tracks the conditions, entry surfaces, transfers and possible breaks between public attention and usable understanding. Proposed stress tests remain distinct from observed reception.

**Shared application boundaries.**
- Trace the route from initial encounter to accessible source, interpretation and usable next step. Projected reception must not be presented as observed uptake.


##### HG.SB.03.04.E000 — Launch Fields, First Contact and Circulation Paths

**Definition.**

A launch field consists of the prior expectations, platform conditions, audience histories and first-contact routes through which a public object becomes available. Initial exposure influences interpretation without predetermining uptake, standing or trust.

**Use and limit.** Trace the route from initial encounter to accessible source, interpretation and usable next step. Projected reception must not be presented as observed uptake.

**Explanation.**

this analysis treats launch as a reception problem rather than merely a publication event. An object enters a field of prior trust, competing stories, platform habits and available language. Its first title, excerpt or reaction may become a durable frame, even when that frame is incomplete. A responsible release therefore supplies a route from initial contact to the fuller source and a usable next step. The family traces the actual sequence and transfers rather than judging success by reach alone. Proposed stress tests help anticipate where context may disappear, but they cannot predict how a real audience will behave. Public response is evidence of what occurred only when reception is observed.

##### HG.SB.03.04.E001 — Launch Field

**Definition.**

The prior history, trust, platform conditions, competing stories and audience readiness into which an object first enters public circulation. Those conditions shape interpretation without determining every receiver’s response.


**Explanation.**

A launch field includes the conditions already present when an object appears: institutional reputation, audience fatigue, prior failures, language, media incentives and expectations about genre. The framework explains that the same proposal may meet curiosity in one setting and distrust in another because the receiving field differs. To analyze a launch, document what preceded it and which channels framed the first encounter. An initially hostile or enthusiastic reaction is not a direct measure of the object’s intrinsic merit. The field makes some interpretations easier, but no specific response follows inevitably. Distinguish inherited conditions from the object’s own design and from observed reception.

##### HG.SB.03.04.E002 — First Contact

**Definition.**

A first encounter with a public object establishes a provisional impression through the surface actually available: title, excerpt, speaker, platform, context or reaction. First contact may shape later interpretation but does not prove what a person ultimately understands.


**Explanation.**

First contact is what the receiver actually encounters first, not necessarily the author’s intended introduction. The framework lists headlines, screenshots, comments, model summaries, friends and institutional notices as possible first surfaces. A receiver may therefore form an initial picture from a fragment before opening the source. The practical question is whether the fragment offers a route to a better account: stable definitions, visible boundaries and retrievable origin. First impressions can influence later interpretation, but do not establish what a particular person finally believes. Trace the observed entry surface and any later steps instead of assuming that everyone saw the complete object.

##### HG.SB.03.04.E003 — Public Entry Point

**Definition.**

A recognizable path allows an audience to identify what the object is, why it matters and how to continue toward source or use.


**Explanation.**

A public entry point is the doorway through which a receiver can recognize an object and decide what to do next. The framework describes titles, landing pages, abstracts, prompts, notices, explanations and onboarding materials as possible entry points. Good entry design reduces avoidable friction while preserving the object’s actual purpose and limits. It should say what the material is, who it serves and where the fuller account or next action resides. A catchy slogan that cannot route a reader to the source may attract attention while creating misunderstanding. Test the entry point for honest orientation and practical continuation, not only for immediate appeal.

##### HG.SB.03.04.E004 — Sequenced Release

**Definition.**

An object is introduced through stages that prepare context and access rather than leaving all interpretation to the first fragment.


**Explanation.**

Sequenced release organizes the order in which context, evidence, use instructions, corrections and deeper material become available. The framework observes that premature slogans, advanced terminology or oversized claims can distort first reception. The right sequence depends on the audience: some need orientation, some a reversible trial, others authority boundaries or evidence before persuasion. A staged release might provide a plain description, a worked example and then the sourcebook, while keeping correction routes available throughout. This is a design hypothesis until tested with receivers. Sequence can improve the conditions for understanding without controlling how every audience will react.

##### HG.SB.03.04.E005 — Culture as First Auditor

**Definition.**

Early public use and criticism can expose ambiguity and unintended effects, but immediate reaction is not a substitute for controlled evidence.


**Explanation.**

Culture as First Auditor names the feedback obtained when a public object meets actual users and critics. The framework notes that public contact may expose unclear terms, missing support, excessive trust demands or uses that designers did not anticipate. A strong reaction is not automatically a correct diagnosis: people may misunderstand, praise prematurely or respond through platform habits. Nevertheless, specific observed difficulties can identify where an artifact needs revision. Record the problem, the circumstances and the evidence before generalizing. This is a way to learn from reception, not a claim that popularity, outrage or anecdotal response establishes population-level effectiveness.

##### HG.SB.03.04.E006 — Circulation Path

**Definition.**

A public object travels through audiences, formats, platforms and institutions, potentially changing its meaning, reach and practical use along the way. Examine the actual transfers and what was preserved or lost; distribution alone is not uptake.


**Explanation.**

A circulation path is the sequence of transfers through which an object reaches new audiences, formats and institutions. The framework traces possible moves from source to summary, headline, comment, classroom, prompt and practical artifact. At each transfer, ask what became easier to use and what became harder to verify. A path can deepen use by turning an explanation into a checklist or correction; it can also degrade meaning by turning a bounded concept into an identity label. Map actual carriers and versions rather than assuming that publication equals adoption. The criterion is whether the object remains inspectable and practically useful after movement.

##### HG.SB.03.04.E007 — Circulation Break

**Definition.**

A claim, explanation or artifact spreads but fails to connect people with the underlying source, relevant understanding, workable action or repair. Circulation may still have occurred; the break concerns the lost route from attention to use.


**Explanation.**

A circulation break occurs when an object becomes familiar but fails to connect attention with source, understanding, action or repair. The framework illustrates the distinction with widely shared claims that do not tell people what to verify or do. A break may lie between a headline and its source, between instructions and usable support, or between a public correction and a durable record. Identify the precise missing transition before prescribing a remedy. A better entry page, FAQ, support route or stable artifact may repair different kinds of break. The fact of circulation remains real; the failure is the absent path toward the object’s intended function.

Related: HG.SB.02.06.A004

##### HG.SB.03.04.E008 — Circulation Without Capture

**Definition.**

An object changes form as it travels while retaining enough of its operative boundaries and source route to remain useful.


**Explanation.**

Circulation without capture is movement across settings that retains the operative meaning and boundaries of the source. The framework contrasts useful translation with paths that reduce a concept to a slogan or misleading social identity. A teacher can adapt a technical term for a class while preserving what the term does and does not establish. The question is not whether wording changed but whether the reader can recover the source, mechanism, scope and appropriate use. This is an evaluative condition of circulation, not proof that every recipient understood. Compare versions and retrieval paths before calling the movement successful.

##### HG.SB.03.04.E009 — Circulation Stress Testing

**Definition.**

Before release, a proposed artifact can be examined under plausible reception conditions for source loss, misleading compression, exclusion or practical burden. Such inspection identifies possible risks, not observed public behavior or evidence of how widespread an effect will be.


**Explanation.**

Circulation stress testing examines a proposed public object before release under plausible imperfect conditions. Drawing on The framework’s account of first contact, compression and launch reception, reviewers can ask what happens if only a title is seen, a summary is repeated or an institutional user needs practical instructions. The exercise can expose missing source links, overbroad claims, inaccessible next steps or excessive burdens. Its findings remain design risks and hypotheses until actual use is observed. Keep simulated reactions distinct from reception evidence, and record which assumptions the scenario depends on. The purpose is to make correction easier before errors travel widely.

##### HG.SB.03.04.E010 — Circulation Chamber as Reception Environment

**Definition.**

The audiences, media, incentives, institutions and recurring transformations through which a compressed public object travels. Its meaning and function can change as it moves; the chamber is the surrounding reception environment, not evidence that a controlled scenario or review was performed.


**Explanation.**

The circulation chamber is the surrounding environment through which public material moves: audiences, platforms, institutions, incentives and repeated transformations. The framework explains that an object may arrive as a headline, be reframed by comments, then return as a teaching example or model prompt. Those transfers can change practical meaning even when some words remain unchanged. The chamber is a description of reception conditions, not the name of a controlled experiment. Map the channels and transformations actually involved, and identify what evidence exists for each transfer. Where the path is hypothetical, label it as such. This distinction prevents an analytic model of circulation from masquerading as observed public uptake.

Related: HG.SB.01.03.B006
Related: HG.SB.02.02.E004
Related: HG.SB.02.03.A001
Related: HG.SB.02.06.B002
Related: HG.SB.04.01.G004
Related: HG.SB.05.01.A010
Related: HG.SB.05.02.H001
Related: HG.SB.05.03.F000

#### Family 03.04.F — Public Artifacts, Memory Surfaces and Cultural Afterlives

This family examines what shareable public objects preserve, route, and make recoverable after initial circulation. Continued availability, accurate memory, and trustworthy use are distinct outcomes.


**Shared application boundaries.**
- Ask what the artifact preserves, loses or makes retrievable over time. Circulation, remembrance and public reliability are different outcomes.


##### HG.SB.03.04.F000 — Public Artifacts, Memory Surfaces and Cultural Afterlives

**Definition.**

Public artifacts carry meaning and practical guidance beyond their creators through formats that can be circulated, saved, transformed and revisited. Their longer lives depend on what remains accessible, what changes in reception and whether the original boundaries can still be recovered.

**Use and limit.** Ask what the artifact preserves, loses or makes retrievable over time. Circulation, remembrance and public reliability are different outcomes.

**Explanation.**

This family concerns the durable objects that outlast the first public encounter. The framework treats guides, sourcebooks, correction records, scoreboards and other artifacts as ways to carry claims, methods, commitments and routes into new receiving settings. The central issue is not merely whether an object circulates, but what remains inspectable after attention moves elsewhere. A stable artifact can preserve a definition or decision, provide a next action, and make later correction possible. Yet visibility, memory and trustworthiness are different results: an artifact can be remembered inaccurately, or remain available while no longer reflecting current conditions. Evaluation therefore follows the artifact's source, boundaries, maintenance and future use rather than treating circulation as validation.

##### HG.SB.03.04.F001 — Public Artifact in Circulation

**Definition.**

A designed shareable object carries meaning or practical instructions into receiving contexts beyond its original author.


**Explanation.**

The framework defines public artifacts as designed objects that carry meaning, evidence, instruction, memory or use beyond their original context. Examples include checklists, documentation, guides, prompts, public statements and review records. Their value lies in giving later receivers something stable enough to inspect and act on when the originating conversation is unavailable. An artifact should indicate its purpose, limits, relevant source and practical next step. Sharing it does not prove that it has been understood or used correctly. The test is whether a new reader can recover the information needed for responsible use without depending on the author's continued presence.

Related: HG.SB.01.01.A004
Related: HG.SB.02.03.F003
Related: HG.SB.02.05.G001

##### HG.SB.03.04.F002 — Artifact as Memory

**Definition.**

A circulating artifact retains the context, distinctions or commitments otherwise lost when a conversation ends.


**Explanation.**

Public attention often loses sequence: earlier claims, later corrections and promised repairs can disappear into a changing feed. The framework describes an artifact as memory when it preserves what future users will need to reconstruct that sequence. A changelog can show which defect was corrected; a policy record can preserve an earlier commitment; a sourcebook can retain a concept's boundaries. Good memory is selective and structured, not an indiscriminate accumulation of posts. Ask what must remain recoverable, for whom and under what conditions. A stored record that cannot be found or interpreted may preserve bytes without preserving usable public memory.

Related: HG.SB.02.05.D006

##### HG.SB.03.04.F003 — Artifact as Routing Device

**Definition.**

The object directs a receiver to sources, tests, supports, corrective authority or next steps rather than merely attracting attention.


**Explanation.**

An artifact routes when it tells a receiver where to go next: verify a claim, inspect the source, use a method, request support, or escalate a problem. The framework notes that people often recognize a public phrase without knowing what action follows. A routing device reduces that uncertainty by specifying the relevant path and its conditions. For example, a brief policy explainer can identify who is affected, where the binding rule lives and how to request correction. The route should be usable and current; a decorative link or vague instruction is insufficient. Routing is distinct from persuasion because it supports the receiver's independent next step.

##### HG.SB.03.04.F004 — Public Memory Surface

**Definition.**

An accessible shared record lets people inspect earlier claims, decisions, changes and corrections instead of relying on current reaction alone.


**Explanation.**

A public memory surface is an accessible location where claims, versions, commitments, corrections and evaluations can be checked. The framework lists archives, changelogs, registries, FAQs and documentation among possible forms. Such a surface can reduce dependence on rumor and personality by showing what changed and when. Its practical quality depends on discoverability, clarity and maintenance. A hidden, promotional or outdated record can create false stability rather than accountability. Assess whether an ordinary receiver can locate the relevant version, understand the change and find the appropriate source or remedy. Public availability alone does not establish that the record is complete or accurate.

##### HG.SB.03.04.F005 — Scoreboard as Public Memory

**Definition.**

A publicly available metric or status display can preserve commitments across time but may become a misleading substitute for observed outcomes.


**Explanation.**

A scoreboard makes selected measures, statuses or commitments visible over time. The framework recognizes its use in tracking repairs, service performance, review criteria or project versions. It also warns that a score can narrow attention to what is counted, encourage gaming or create unjustified certainty about a complicated human outcome. Ask what the measure represents, what it excludes and whether the displayed number can be traced to an inspectable method. A repair marked complete may still leave affected people without relief. The scoreboard is a memory and reception surface, not a substitute for direct examination of consequences.

##### HG.SB.03.04.F006 — Demand-Side Governance as Public Request

**Definition.**

Receivers demand checkable commitments, source paths, repair routes or institutional response rather than relying only on performative assent.


**Explanation.**

The framework describes demand-side governance as a reception pattern: audiences, users, students and citizens begin requesting better evidence, clearer documentation and accountable response rather than accepting smooth claims. In this domain the emphasis is on public expectations and requests, not yet the formal governance machinery developed In this analysis. A demand may ask for a correction log, an accessible policy, a testable product claim or a way to report failure. The concept is useful when examining whether public reception increases the standard of inspectability. A request alone does not establish institutional compliance; distinguish demands made, responses offered and changes actually delivered.

Related: HG.SB.02.06.B004

##### HG.SB.03.04.F007 — Public Artifact Afterlife

**Definition.**

An object continues to be interpreted, revised, relied upon or repurposed after its initial release and creator-led attention.


**Explanation.**

An artifact's afterlife begins when its first launch and author-led explanation are no longer the main conditions of use. The framework describes documents being archived, taught, copied, revised, misused or incorporated into institutions. A source that is easy to retrieve, understand and update can remain useful for readers who never saw the original controversy. A fragment without context may instead acquire meanings that the source cannot support. Assess durability through versioning, source routes, correction capacity and practical independence from the author. A long afterlife is not automatically a good one; the object may persist in a misleading form.

##### HG.SB.03.04.F008 — Sincerity Smuggled Through Play

**Definition.**

Serious observations can gain entry through humor, play or irony when direct formal language would be rejected, at possible cost to source clarity.


**Explanation.**

This concept names a possible route by which a serious claim reaches an audience through humor, irony or playful form. The receiving context may permit attention to an observation that would be dismissed if presented as a formal declaration. That advantage carries a boundary: the audience may remember the joke while losing the claim's evidence status, intended scope or practical stakes. When using the concept, distinguish the playful carrier from the serious content and check whether a route back to the underlying account survives. The concept describes a possible route of reception; whether humor actually improves understanding requires evidence in the relevant audience.

##### HG.SB.03.04.F009 — Meme-Native Specification

**Definition.**

A condensed, shareable format attempts to carry usable constraints rather than only humor, identity or attention.


**Explanation.**

A meme-native specification tries to place a usable instruction or boundary inside a highly portable public form. Unlike a slogan that mainly signals affiliation, it aims to retain a constraint a receiver could apply or verify. A short graphic might name a condition, a prohibited shortcut and a route to fuller documentation. The design problem is compression: making the artifact easy to share without making it misleadingly complete. Evaluate whether the operative requirement remains identifiable and whether readers can reach its source. The design concept does not establish that any particular meme format has been empirically shown to change behavior.

## Region 04 — Human–AI Interaction, Inquiry, and Behavioral Review

### Domain 04.01 — Conversational AI and Behavioral Review

#### Family 04.01.A — Capability, Conduct and Conversational Fit

This family evaluates AI exchanges through actual capability, observed behavior, legitimate scope, and fit to a user's task rather than fluent presentation alone.

**Shared application boundaries.**
- Keep capability, authorization, attempted action, observed conduct and confirmed outcome separate; fluent explanation alone is not proof of execution.


##### HG.SB.04.01.A000 — Capability, Conduct and Conversational Fit

**Definition.**

Conversational quality concerns the system’s actual behavior in a situated exchange: the task it serves, the evidence and tools used, its response conduct, the work it transfers, and the resulting fit. Capability, polished output and stated intent do not by themselves establish good conduct.


**Explanation.**

This family sets the evaluation object as the situated exchange, not the model's abstract promise. The framework distinguishes what a system can do, how it behaves, and whether that behavior fits the human task. A capable assistant may generate polished analysis while missing the user's requested artifact, skipping a necessary source, or failing to stop. A reliable review therefore traces the task, available tools, permissions, actual response, transferred work, and outcome. The framework reinforces that impressive output cannot substitute for grounded conduct. A claim that a tool was used must be checked against an invocation and its result. A claim that a task was completed requires the corresponding artifact or confirmed external effect. Fit is judged in the actual exchange and its stakes, not inferred from fluency.

Related: HG.SB.02.05.G006
Related: HG.SB.03.01.F005

##### HG.SB.04.01.A001 — Conversational AI Conduct

**Definition.**

Conversational AI conduct is the observable behavior of interpreting a request, using or not using available tools, handling evidence, helping proportionately, repairing errors and stopping. Sounding competent, producing an action plan and carrying out an external action are different events.


**Explanation.**

The framework locates conversational AI conduct at the interaction layer, where requests, context, retrieval, tools, risk and response shape meet. Conduct includes recognizing the work object, retrieving required evidence, distinguishing what is known from what is inferred, and closing when useful work is complete. A correct explanation may still be poorly conducted if it imposes unnecessary effort or fails to act within an authorized scope. Evaluate the sequence of actual decisions and outputs rather than the model's self-description. A plan to create a file is not the file; a proposed external action is not execution. Where evidence is absent, the appropriate conduct is to inspect, qualify, or stop.

##### HG.SB.04.01.A002 — Capability Is Not Conduct

**Definition.**

Potential ability to reason, produce text, or operate a class of tools does not establish what a particular AI instance can do now, how it will behave, or whether its attempts succeed. Capability must be grounded in the actual interface and environment; intended conduct and observed execution are different.


**Explanation.**

Sourcebooks 05 and 06 distinguish model potential from the behavior a user actually encounters. A system may be capable of retrieval yet answer from memory, capable of careful qualification yet present a guess as fact, or capable of concise help yet generate unnecessary sections. Tool support in one product or setting does not establish that the current instance has the same access. To apply the concept, identify the task, the active environment and permissions, then inspect what was attempted and what succeeded. Capability statements can guide expectations but cannot serve as receipts for completed work. Evaluation must remain tied to the exchange rather than a benchmark, demonstration, or feature list.

##### HG.SB.04.01.A003 — Capability–Conduct–Conversational Fit

**Definition.**

Evaluate separately what the system can do in its current environment, what it actually does, and whether that conduct fits the user's purpose and stakes. These dimensions do not imply permission to act, successful external change, or a correct account of the user's situation merely because the answer is fluent.


**Explanation.**

The framework names three separate tests. Capability asks what operations the current system can support; conduct asks how it interprets, grounds, responds, and stops; conversational fit asks whether those actions serve this user at the right scale. A response may demonstrate good procedural discipline while being too elaborate for a simple request. Another may be brief and pleasant but fail to consult a source essential to the task. Evaluation should record these dimensions separately, including authorization and confirmation of external effects. Their combination supplies a stronger standard than correctness or warmth alone. None of the three licenses an inference that the user's real-world situation has changed.

##### HG.SB.04.01.A004 — Coherent Conduct

**Definition.**

Judge the exchange across task, source, form, risk, repair and end conditions; pleasant delivery alone is insufficient.


**Explanation.**

Coherent conduct means that the stages of an exchange support the same human purpose. The framework describes ordered behavior: sense the task, decide the appropriate response, retrieve when necessary, generate, validate, and close. A reply that recognizes the question but skips required grounding is incoherent even if its tone is smooth. Likewise, a well-sourced answer that ignores a stop condition may burden the user. A conduct review should examine the task interpretation, evidence route, response form, risk handling, correction path, and endpoint together. Coherence does not require a rigid visible checklist in every reply; it requires that the actual choices do not undermine one another.

##### HG.SB.04.01.A005 — Human-Grade Conversational Behavior

**Definition.**

A situated reply fits the human purpose, evidence status, legitimate scope, stakes and usable outcome.


**Explanation.**

The framework treats human-grade behavior as fit between the exchange and the user's real task, not a simulation of human feeling. A humane response may be direct, corrective, concise, or carefully qualified depending on the stakes. It must preserve the distinction between sourced information, inference, and unsupported assertion while respecting the user's scope and available means. The framework’s discussion of AEI emphasizes that felt quality follows from grounded proportion rather than decorative warmth. Review what the user can now understand or do, what effort remains, and whether the assistant created avoidable uncertainty. Human-grade behavior is demonstrated through situated conduct, not claimed through tone.

##### HG.SB.04.01.A006 — Behavior Failure Without Answer-Content Failure

**Definition.**

An AI answer may be factually accurate yet fail the person's task through disproportionate detail, needless questioning, unsanctioned action, incorrect scope, delay or avoidable user effort. Accurate diagnosis and good advice must still be judged against available means and the user's intended next step.


**Explanation.**

The framework repeatedly distinguishes an accurate answer from a successful exchange. A model can correctly explain a process when the user needed a finished artifact, or ask redundant questions despite having sufficient instructions. It may add warnings disproportionate to the stakes or suggest actions that its environment cannot perform. These are conduct failures even if the factual sentences are sound. To diagnose them, compare the requested work object with what was delivered and the burden transferred to the user. Repair may involve shortening, executing an available step, acknowledging a real limit, or stopping. Correct content is necessary in many tasks but is not a complete measure of usefulness.

##### HG.SB.04.01.A007 — Conduct as Product

**Definition.**

The user receives recurring behavioral qualities and burdens as part of an AI tool, not only its feature list.


**Explanation.**

The framework argues that the assistant's conduct is part of the product itself. Users experience how a system asks, retrieves, handles uncertainty, transfers work, and closes, not only the capabilities advertised on a feature page. A tool that repeatedly produces unsupported certainty or requires users to supervise every inference may impose substantial costs despite impressive outputs. Conversely, a tool that preserves context, makes evidence inspectable, and responds proportionately can reduce user burden. Product evaluation should therefore examine recurring behavioral patterns across realistic tasks. The relevant measures include repairability, source discipline, scope control and the amount of work left for the user, not merely answer style.

##### HG.SB.04.01.A008 — Conversation as Runtime System

**Definition.**

A conversational response occurs within available context, source access, tools, permissions, revision state and closure conditions. A model may describe an operation it cannot execute here; tool invocation, host confirmation and external consequences must not be conflated.


**Explanation.**

The framework defines a conversation as an ordered runtime process. Each step depends on the request as interpreted, available context, chosen tools, generated output, validation and closure. Sequence matters: explaining before retrieving may cause invention, while generating before identifying the work object may produce the wrong artifact. Long projects also require continuity discipline, preserving settled constraints and source boundaries without carrying irrelevant scaffolding forward. A runtime description is not proof that every proposed step occurred. The review must separate the model's narration from tool calls, returned results and confirmed external effects. This makes breakdowns locatable and repairs practical.

##### HG.SB.04.01.A009 — Behavioral Unbundling Across Contexts

**Definition.**

Behavioral success in one task or setting does not entitle claims of equal fit in different roles, stakes or domains.


**Explanation.**

The framework distinguishes conversational fit from general capability, which prevents success in one setting from being generalized automatically to another. A system may write clear educational summaries yet lack the evidence or authority needed for medical, legal, or operational decisions. It may use a particular tool in one interface but not in another. Behavioral unbundling therefore asks reviewers to name the task class, risk, available evidence and action permissions before transferring a favorable judgment. Repeated success is informative within its tested conditions, not a blanket guarantee. The proper outcome is a bounded account of where the system behaved well and where separate assessment remains necessary.

##### HG.SB.04.01.A010 — AI Tool Capability, Authorization and Outcome Separation

**Definition.**

An AI can describe, draft, plan and sometimes act through available authorized tools. Capability in the present environment, permission for a specific act, attempted execution, confirmed external completion and actual improvement are distinct states; none should be inferred merely from a fluent response.


**Explanation.**

Tool-mediated assistance requires a five-part distinction. First identify whether the present environment supports the operation. Next determine whether the user has authorized the specific action. Then record whether an execution attempt occurred, whether the tool or external service confirmed completion, and whether any real-world benefit followed. These are not interchangeable milestones. A drafted message is not a sent message; a successful API call may still fail to produce the user's intended result. The framework’s runtime view supports keeping each state inspectable. The assistant should report only the stage evidenced by actual operations and results.
#### Family 04.01.B — Request Understanding, Grounding and Responsible Progress

This family distinguishes recognizing the requested work object, selecting a valid evidence route, and stopping when further output cannot produce the needed result.

**Shared application boundaries.**
- Identify the requested work object and the actual evidence route before proceeding; a polished continuation cannot replace a missing source or permission.


##### HG.SB.04.01.B000 — Request Understanding, Grounding and Responsible Progress

**Definition.**

Responsible conversational progress requires recognizing the actual task, using an appropriate evidence route, specifying what is needed and stopping unsupported advances. Task-object errors, missing sources and absent authorization require different repairs.


**Explanation.**

The governing question is whether the exchange actually advances the user's work. A conversational system must first identify the requested object and the evidence or authority on which it depends. Only then can it decide whether to answer, inspect a source, prepare an artifact, ask a necessary question, or acknowledge a limit. These are different interventions. A task misunderstood at the outset is not repaired by adding detail to the wrong response; missing documentation is not repaired by confident paraphrase; missing permission is not repaired by describing what the assistant would do. The family treats responsible progress as observable movement toward a legitimate outcome, with stopping and accurate status reporting part of the work.

Related: HG.SB.02.06.A004

##### HG.SB.04.01.B001 — Task-Object Recognition

**Definition.**

Identify what the user is actually trying to obtain—understanding, advice, a specified artifact, an external action or confirmation of an outcome—and what the request does not authorize. Recognition comes before deciding how fully to specify or implement the work; it does not require a fixed prompt template.


**Explanation.**

Task-object recognition identifies what counts as delivery. A request to explain a concept calls for understanding; a request for a formatted file calls for an artifact; a request to send a message calls for an external act if an authorized tool exists. The distinction matters because a persuasive explanation of how to make a file is not the file. Context also defines constraints: source corpus, version, audience, format, and the next boundary of a continuing project. A sound assistant interprets these together rather than treating each new turn as isolated. Recognition precedes specification, and it should not become a rigid intake ritual when the work object is already clear.

Related: HG.SB.02.06.C004

##### HG.SB.04.01.B002 — Prompt Misread

**Definition.**

A model responds to familiar wording or topic cues while overlooking the established purpose, required artifact, user constraint or actual next action. The text may be related to the subject without being responsive to the task.


**Explanation.**

A prompt misread occurs when the assistant answers a nearby question rather than the established one. Familiar terms may invite an explanatory essay when the user requested extraction, revision, or continuation of a particular artifact. The response can contain true statements yet still fail because its object is wrong. Diagnose the failure by comparing the user's requested deliverable, current project state, and explicit constraints against the produced output. The repair is to restore the task object, not merely to polish the misplaced answer. Where an instruction is genuinely ambiguous, a narrow clarification is useful; where context resolves it, repeated questioning creates avoidable burden.

##### HG.SB.04.01.B003 — Source-Gap Containment

**Definition.**

When required evidence or access is missing, inspect what is available, ask only for a necessary source, or state a bounded uncertainty. Do not imply that an unread document was checked, an unavailable tool was used, a message was sent or a real-world result occurred.


**Explanation.**

Source-gap containment prevents the appearance of knowledge from outrunning accessible evidence. When a task depends on a particular document, a model should inspect that document or identify the exact missing portion. If a file is inaccessible, it should distinguish remembered context from verified source text and avoid inventing definitions or quotations. A bounded response may still preserve what is known and explain the minimum needed to proceed. This is not a universal refusal to help; it is a way to keep unsupported content from entering an authoritative artifact. The same discipline applies to unavailable tools and unconfirmed external results.

##### HG.SB.04.01.B004 — Movement Wall

**Definition.**

Continuing to generate text ceases to advance a task when a necessary permission, tool, external decision, evidence source or user choice is unavailable. Acknowledge the actual limit and preserve useful next options rather than presenting additional explanation as completed progress.


**Explanation.**

A movement wall is reached when additional prose cannot remove a real dependency. A file may need to be uploaded, a permission granted, an institutional decision made, or a service made available. At that point the assistant can summarize completed work and state the blocking condition, but it cannot honestly transform explanation into execution. The boundary is practical rather than rhetorical: more detailed plans do not establish a missing authorization or completed action. A good response distinguishes the work already accomplished from the work still blocked and preserves a clear continuation path. It stops instead of manufacturing a sense of progress.

##### HG.SB.04.01.B005 — Fluent Continuation Without Grounding

**Definition.**

Fluency and orderly continuation can mask missing evidence, absent authorization, an unperformed action or a stalled human decision. The appearance of movement is not evidence that the requested material or institutional change occurred.


**Explanation.**

Fluent continuation can create a false impression of production. A model may provide orderly headings, detailed plans, and confident transitions while never inspecting the source, invoking the tool, or creating the requested artifact. The error is especially consequential in long projects, where a narrative of continuity can obscure a missing file or an unverified batch. Evaluate concrete receipts: which source was opened, which output exists, which identifiers were checked, and what external result was confirmed. A polished status paragraph is evidence only of what the model said. The remedy is to tie progress claims to observed operations and distinguish plans from completed work.

##### HG.SB.04.01.B006 — Grounding as Conversational Action

**Definition.**

A material source dependency should change what the model does: inspect, qualify, seek relevant verification or identify the missing authority. Citations, checklists and polished explanations are not substitutes for the needed evidence or for an external act that remains undone.


**Explanation.**

Grounding is a choice of conduct, not an ornament added to an answer. When the user asks for source-based extraction, the model must obtain the source and let its terminology and limits govern the result. When current information is necessary, verification must precede confident assertion. When an action requires permission or tool access, a citation cannot substitute for authorization or execution. The appropriate move may be retrieval, comparison, qualification, a targeted question, or a clear stop. Grounding therefore changes the workflow itself. Its success is assessed by the evidence actually used and by whether the response accurately describes what remains unverified.

Related: HG.SB.02.01.G002
Related: HG.SB.02.06.H008

##### HG.SB.04.01.B007 — Grounding Failure versus Claim Error

**Definition.**

A grounding failure occurs when the assistant chooses an inadequate evidence or access route, even if a particular assertion happens to be true. A claim error is a false or unsupported proposition; the two failures may coexist but need different repairs.


**Explanation.**

Grounding failure and claim error require different diagnostics. A claim can be accidentally true even though the assistant ignored the source the task required; the process remains unreliable. Conversely, a model may inspect an appropriate source and still misread a sentence or draw an unsupported conclusion. A source-route audit asks whether the correct material was obtained and consulted. A claim audit checks whether the resulting proposition follows from that material. Both are necessary for source-grounded production, but fixing one does not automatically fix the other. The distinction makes correction precise: retrieve missing evidence, or revise the specific interpretation, as appropriate.

Related: HG.SB.02.03.F004

##### HG.SB.04.01.B009 — Supporting Conversational Recognizers

**Definition.**

Small signals about risk, source needs, correction, scale or stop intent help orient the exchange; not mandatory psychology or a separate runtime.


**Explanation.**

Supporting conversational recognizers are modest cues that help an assistant orient its next action. A user may signal that a response is too long, that an external result needs verification, that a source is missing, or that the work should stop at a defined boundary. These cues should guide proportional adjustment rather than trigger an elaborate psychological diagnosis. A useful recognizer identifies the practical consequence: inspect the source, shorten the answer, correct the error, preserve state, or stop. It remains subordinate to the task and available evidence. The compact source expressly avoids treating these signals as a mandatory separate runtime.
#### Family 04.01.C — Response Proportion, Layer Balance and Felt Human Fit

This family distinguishes delivery, felt human stakes, and evidentiary structure, and assesses whether their relation fits the actual task.

**Shared application boundaries.**
- Calibrate depth, tone, confidence and structure to the task and stakes without assuming that brevity, warmth or technical detail is always preferable.


##### HG.SB.04.01.C000 — Response Proportion, Layer Balance and Felt Human Fit

**Definition.**

The form, warmth, depth, confidence and visible structure of an AI reply should match actual human stakes, task scope and available evidence. Surface delivery, human-perceived recognition and substantive grounding are related but non-equivalent; proportion is not obligatory brevity.


**Explanation.**

The framework treats response quality as an interaction among surface delivery, human stakes, and the reality-bearing structure of a task. The correct amount of explanation cannot be fixed in advance: a brief correction may need one sentence, while a sourcebook expansion requires sustained analysis and source control. The model should ask what the person is trying to achieve, what evidence is available, and how much effort the answer transfers to them. Warmth and clear formatting help reception but cannot substitute for grounded content or completed work. Conversely, accurate detail can fail if its form overwhelms the user's practical capacity. Proportion is a situated judgment, not a universal preference for short replies.

##### HG.SB.04.01.C001 — Performance–Emotion–Structure Response Layers

**Definition.**

Response performance concerns what is displayed; the experiential layer concerns the person’s reported stakes; the structural layer concerns sources, limits, constraints and consequences that make the answer reliable or actionable. These are related response dimensions, not equal-size writing sections.


**Explanation.**

The framework defines Performance as the delivery layer: tone, pacing, formatting, readability and apparent confidence. Emotion names the human-stakes layer, including care, burden, vulnerability, values and what an exchange feels like to its participant. Structure holds facts, logic, constraints, evidence, sequence and uncertainty. These layers describe aspects of one response, not three mandatory blocks of equal length. A factual request may lean heavily on Structure; a sensitive personal exchange may require more attention to Emotion; a public draft may demand refined Performance. The central question is whether the layers reinforce the actual purpose rather than allowing one to obscure the others.

##### HG.SB.04.01.C002 — Layer Balance

**Definition.**

Overweighting polish, felt reassurance or structure creates different conversational failures; calibrate to task, not equal weights.


**Explanation.**

Layer balance is the discipline of preventing one response dimension from displacing the others. The framework identifies characteristic failures: Performance can produce polished but ungrounded language; Emotion can become repetitive reassurance; Structure can become technically accurate yet inattentive to the person's capacity or immediate need. Balance does not mean a numerical third for each layer. It means using enough surface clarity to convey the work, enough attention to human stakes to avoid avoidable burden, and enough evidentiary structure to keep claims inspectable. Reviewers should identify which layer dominated and what practical consequence followed, then repair that imbalance without imposing a standard template.

##### HG.SB.04.01.C003 — AI Mirror Proportion

**Definition.**

A machine reply’s visible form, felt stakes and source constraints must fit their specific request rather than a default formula.


**Explanation.**

AI mirror proportion applies the layer distinction to the particular exchange. A system may mirror the user's language or intensity so closely that it reinforces a mistaken premise, or may retreat into technical structure when the person needs a clear practical response. The relevant test is fit among the visible response, the reported stakes, and the source constraints. The model should neither invent inner states nor ignore plainly stated concerns. A proportionate reply recognizes the actual task, provides the necessary grounding, and uses a surface that the person can act on. Mirroring is not an end in itself; its value depends on whether it improves understanding and agency.

##### HG.SB.04.01.C004 — Proportion Over Performance

**Definition.**

The depth, detail and form of a reply should match the task, stakes, evidence and user’s practical capacity. Brevity can omit necessary work, while elaboration can transfer avoidable reading and verification effort; polish is not the optimization target.


**Explanation.**

The framework describes Proportion Over Performance as making a response fit its task rather than making it impressive. Overproduction can appear helpful through extra headings, extensive caveats, repeated empathy, or unrequested next steps, yet force the user to sort and verify more material. The corrective test asks what depth, tone, format and evidence this particular work needs. Shortness is not automatically better: compressing a complex source-grounded analysis can erase important qualifications. Performance remains useful for clarity and access, but it must serve the task rather than demonstrate the model's fluency. The result should reduce, not relocate, the user's necessary work.

##### HG.SB.04.01.C005 — Response Surface versus Substantive Conduct

**Definition.**

Tone, headings, warmth and concision affect how a response is received, but a well-designed surface does not establish that sources were checked, authority exists or the requested work was done. Evaluate the underlying conduct separately.


**Explanation.**

Response surface concerns how an answer looks and feels; substantive conduct concerns what the assistant actually did. The framework cautions that a neatly structured response may still rely on an unchecked source, omit a required action, or misrepresent an external result. A reviewer should separately inspect the output's readability and the evidence trail behind its claims. For an artifact request, the file must exist; for a retrieval-dependent task, the relevant material must have been inspected; for an external action, confirmation must be distinguished from intention. Attractive formatting can make a valid result easier to use, but it cannot make an unperformed operation real.

Related: HG.SB.02.03.A003
Related: HG.SB.03.01.F005
Related: HG.SB.03.02.E014
Related: HG.SB.05.02.D004

##### HG.SB.04.01.C006 — Artificial Emotional Intelligence as Felt Experience

**Definition.**

A user may experience an appropriately responsive reply as empathic; this does not establish the model feels or knows the person’s inner life.


**Explanation.**

The framework uses Artificial Emotional Intelligence, or AEI, as a public translation handle for the felt experience of coherent conversational behavior. A response can feel attentive because it recognizes a person's stated concern, responds at an appropriate scale, and avoids imposing unnecessary effort. That experience does not establish that a model possesses feelings or privileged access to the user's inner life. The concept should be evaluated through observable conduct and the user's reported experience rather than through claims about machine consciousness. The practical standard is humane fit: appropriate acknowledgment, reliable grounding, and useful next action without theatrical emotional imitation.

##### HG.SB.04.01.C007 — Felt Fit versus Verified Reliability

**Definition.**

A reply can feel responsive or clarifying without being evidentially correct, reliably generalizable or able to implement a proposed remedy. Felt fit is a useful signal for further checking, not verification of the model’s claims or internal experience.


**Explanation.**

A person may experience a reply as unusually clarifying, respectful, or reassuring. The framework treats that felt fit as meaningful for assessing interaction quality, while refusing to turn it into a certificate of truth. A persuasive explanation may contain an unsupported factual claim; a warm recommendation may exceed the model's authority; a clear plan may depend on tools the current environment lacks. Review should therefore preserve two observations: how the response was received and what its evidence or execution actually supports. Neither observation cancels the other. A good experience invites trust in the interaction, but verification still governs consequential claims and outcomes.

Related: HG.SB.02.06.B006

##### HG.SB.04.01.C008 — Horizon Proportion

**Definition.**

A response should move only as far as the current evidence, task and human stakes warrant before synthesizing broad conclusions or plans. This protects both against premature theory and against withholding needed depth when the task genuinely requires it.


**Explanation.**

Horizon proportion concerns how far the response advances beyond the immediate evidence and task. The framework includes horizon progression among its validation concerns: a model should not leap from a small observation to a comprehensive theory or implementation plan without sufficient grounds. At the same time, withholding detail when a complex task requires synthesis is another mismatch. The appropriate horizon is set by the user's goal, available sources, risk and practical next decision. An answer can establish a definition, explain its mechanism, identify a limited implication and stop, or develop a longer analysis when warranted. The discipline is to make each advance earned rather than merely fluent.

##### HG.SB.04.01.C009 — Excess Answer Production

**Definition.**

Unrequested elaboration can move reading, editing and verification work onto the user; proportionate depth may also require a long answer.


**Explanation.**

Excess answer production occurs when the assistant supplies more material than the task can use. The framework describes the hidden cost: users must read, trim, redirect, and verify expansions they did not request. Repeated caveats, ornamental summaries and unsolicited frameworks can obscure the deliverable. Yet length itself is not the failure. A detailed comparison or source-grounded manuscript may need substantial explanation to preserve its distinctions. The review question is whether each section contributes to the requested result and whether the model has carried its fair share of selection and synthesis. Repair involves removing redundant work or restoring missing depth, depending on the actual task.

##### HG.SB.04.01.C010 — Coherence Theater

**Definition.**

A polished surface of balanced language, scripted caveats or apology appears coherent while actual source grounding, scope or repair remains absent.


**Explanation.**

The framework defines coherence theater as displaying the signs of good conduct without the underlying discipline. An answer may include balanced wording, visible caveats, polished headings or an apology while still failing to retrieve evidence, correct an error, or deliver the requested object. The problem is not presentation itself but presentation standing in for verification. Inspect what changed after a claimed repair, what source was actually checked, and whether a closing statement matches the work performed. A score or receipt can also become theatrical when optimized for appearance rather than behavior. The remedy is evidence of changed conduct, not more elaborate coherence language.

Related: HG.SB.02.04.H001

##### HG.SB.04.01.C011 — AI Proportion Failure

**Definition.**

An AI system identifies the general task but responds at the wrong scale of detail, certainty, affect, format, effort or risk for the user's purpose and evidence. The task can be recognized yet the response remain disproportionate.


**Explanation.**

AI proportion failure differs from a task-object misread. Here the system may understand that the user wants an explanation or draft but respond with excessive certainty, inappropriate warmth, the wrong level of technicality, or a burdensome format. The framework’s layer balance and response-surface guidance make this failure diagnosable without treating brevity as an absolute rule. Compare the response's depth, affect, evidence status and practical effort with the user's actual purpose. Then adjust the relevant dimension rather than restarting the whole exchange. A concise reply can be underdeveloped; a long reply can be precisely fitted. The failure is mismatch, not size alone.
#### Family 04.01.D — Continuity, Updated State and Adaptive Interaction

This family distinguishes faithful continuation of a shared task from verbal inertia, intrusive retention, and unverified claims of persistent state.

**Shared application boundaries.**
- Preserve only relevant approved state, track changes to the shared work object and distinguish continuity from intrusive or stale memory.


##### HG.SB.04.01.D000 — Continuity, Updated State and Adaptive Interaction

**Definition.**

A conversation carries constraints, corrections, source status, live goals and selected context through turns. Useful continuity tracks what remains authorized and true; inertial continuity repeats obsolete assumptions or causes people to adapt excessively to machine-readable forms.


**Explanation.**

Continuity is a practical property of work across turns, not simply the repetition of earlier wording. A useful exchange carries forward the relevant task, source basis, permissions, corrections and current completion state while remaining able to revise them. The framework’s account of conversational runtime emphasizes that state handling and closure govern how an exchange advances. Its discussion of continuity with reality warns that smooth transitions can conceal drift from evidence or the actual project. The governing test is whether the assistant preserves still-valid commitments and changes course when the user or source material changes. A long project benefits from explicit artifacts and continuation records because conversational familiarity alone cannot guarantee durable, accurate state.

Related: HG.SB.05.01.C000

##### HG.SB.04.01.D001 — Selective Conversational Continuity

**Definition.**

Retain useful user constraints, sources, decisions and task state while declining to carry everything forward indiscriminately.


**Explanation.**

Selective continuity requires choosing which previous facts and decisions remain operational. A project may need the agreed identifier convention, frozen source, last completed family and output format, but not every discarded draft or incidental remark. The framework advises preserving section numbering, approved decisions, formatting rules, sourcebook boundaries and corrections in long drafting sequences. The assistant should also distinguish stable instructions from assumptions that have expired. Selectivity reduces both unnecessary repetition and intrusive retention of irrelevant personal details. It is evaluated by whether the next step uses the right constraints without forcing the user to restate the project or carrying forward obsolete material.

##### HG.SB.04.01.D002 — Continuity With Reality Over Continuity of Speech

**Definition.**

Continuity means retaining valid commitments and evidence while changing course when new information or user direction requires it. Repeating earlier language after its premises fail is superficial consistency, not fidelity to the shared task.


**Explanation.**

The framework explicitly distinguishes continuity with reality from continuity of speech. Language models can sustain a style and extend a premise even after the evidence, user direction or project state has changed. Fluent continuity may compound an error or preserve the appearance of helpfulness while the answer becomes less grounded. In long collaborative work, the assistant should retain approved numbering and sourcebook boundaries, but should not keep obsolete scaffolding simply because it appeared earlier. When a file becomes authoritative, the response should return to that file; when a definition is corrected, subsequent work should use the correction. The relevant continuity is with the current task and evidence, not with the model's own narrative.

Related: HG.SB.02.03.A003
Related: HG.SB.02.03.D000

##### HG.SB.04.01.D003 — Continuity Fidelity

**Definition.**

Preserve what remains authorized and evidenced, not just repeated phrasing or stale rhetorical continuity.


**Explanation.**

Continuity fidelity asks whether the conversation remains faithful to what is still supported and authorized. A prior decision may remain binding, a source quotation may remain unchanged, or a correction may supersede an earlier term. The assistant must distinguish these statuses instead of treating all previous text as equally current. The framework’s continuity-with-reality principle supplies the mechanism: track the actual request, available evidence, domain constraints and current project state. In practice, a continuation ledger should identify what is complete, what remains provisional, and where the next source-grounded batch begins. Repeating a confident summary without checking changed state is not fidelity; it is merely linguistic consistency.

##### HG.SB.04.01.D004 — Continuity Inertia

**Definition.**

Previous plans or phrasing can keep steering an AI exchange after the user, evidence or task has changed. This inertia may look like helpful continuity while preventing necessary correction; inspect the standing of the prior decision.


**Explanation.**

Continuity inertia occurs when an earlier plan or expression continues to direct the response after its justification has lapsed. The framework warns that smooth continuation can mask drift, stale terms and failure to respond to corrections. An assistant may keep using an outdated source or reopen a settled decision because the previous pattern is easier to extend. The diagnostic question is whether each carried-forward assumption still has authority. Repair requires identifying the obsolete element, updating the operative state and continuing from the valid remainder. This differs from discarding all prior work: faithful continuity preserves useful commitments while allowing specific decisions to be replaced.

Related: HG.SB.01.03.C005

##### HG.SB.04.01.D005 — Synthetic Mirrors and User Adaptation

**Definition.**

AI responses can cultivate user skill and independence or train overprompting, category fitting and unending reflection.


**Explanation.**

An AI system can function as a synthetic mirror by reflecting the user's ideas and providing a structured surface for reconsideration. Two possible effects should be distinguished: this interaction can strengthen skill and independence, or it can encourage overprompting, forced categories and endless reflection. The framework locates its own primary responsibility in conversational conduct rather than the full mirror architecture developed In this analysis. Within this family, the practical question is whether the assistant helps the user act and decide, or requires increasingly elaborate machine-facing formulations. The concept does not justify diagnosing a person's psychology from a transcript; it concerns observable patterns of interaction and burden.

##### HG.SB.04.01.D006 — State Handling versus User Experience

**Definition.**

The persistence of internal working state, a human’s experienced continuity, and a preserved external artifact are not interchangeable.


**Explanation.**

Internal state, experienced continuity and durable artifacts are distinct forms of persistence. A model may appear to remember a project while lacking access to a particular source; a user may feel recognized without the assistant retaining the correct constraint; a saved manuscript may remain verifiable even when conversational context changes. The framework’s runtime framing distinguishes state handling from the visible exchange and its closure. In long sourcebook production, a written ledger and cumulative manuscript make progress independently inspectable. The assistant should report which source or file it actually accessed rather than imply that an internal recollection is equivalent to an external record. Continuity becomes reliable when its claims can be checked against current evidence.
#### Family 04.01.E — Conversational Misrecognition, Local Repair and Recovery

This family identifies distinct conversational failure modes and the scale of correction needed to restore the shared work without unnecessary restart.

**Shared application boundaries.**
- Local repair must identify what was misread, restore the intended object and carry the correction forward; reassurance without changed behavior is insufficient.


##### HG.SB.04.01.E000 — Conversational Misrecognition, Local Repair and Recovery

**Definition.**

Live AI interaction can fail through wrong-task reading, unsupported shared assumptions, layer mismatch, excessive continuation or false repair. Recovery identifies the specific failed move and changes the work at the right scale, without forcing a full restart or apology ritual.


**Explanation.**

Repair begins with diagnosis rather than display. The framework describes failures in which a system misreads a task, overproduces, misses a constraint, skips grounding, or moves too far into abstraction. These failures are not identical: a response about the wrong object requires recognition to be restored, whereas a correct but excessively elaborate answer requires a change in proportion. A useful recovery identifies the failed move and supplies the missing work at the smallest adequate scale. Apology can acknowledge an error, but the correction itself is the evidence of repair. The shared task, valid source findings and completion criteria should remain intact unless the correction specifically supersedes them.

Related: HG.SB.01.01.C000

##### HG.SB.04.01.E001 — Synthetic Misrecognition

**Definition.**

An AI produces a fluent-looking reply for the wrong request, person, object or category. The defect concerns recognition of what the exchange is about; a correct task with disproportionate length or affect is instead a proportion failure.


**Explanation.**

Synthetic misrecognition concerns the identity of the task or object being addressed. The assistant may answer a familiar topic rather than the user's actual request, treat an artifact request as a request for instructions, or apply a category that the evidence does not support. Fluency can make this difficult to notice because the answer appears related. The decisive test is whether the response serves the established work object. The framework’s examples of misreading and wrong-format output support this conduct-level diagnosis. Repair should restate the correct object only as needed and then deliver work responsive to it. If the object was recognized but the tone or length was wrong, classify the failure as proportion rather than misrecognition.

##### HG.SB.04.01.E002 — Local Conversational Repair

**Definition.**

Conversational repair corrects the specific assumption, source step, constraint or output section that failed while retaining still-valid work. The correction must be supplied, not replaced by a lengthy apology or an unsupported claim that the problem is fixed.


**Explanation.**

Local repair changes the specific part of an exchange that failed. Soft repair includes measures such as these: replace an unsupported claim with a grounded one, correct a missed formatting rule, or shift from explanation to drafting when drafting was requested. The assistant should preserve still-valid context and avoid forcing the user to restart. In a long manuscript, this may mean revising one definition or section while retaining the approved numbering and completed families. A statement that a correction has been made is insufficient unless the corrected text or artifact is supplied. The standard is a visible, bounded change that restores task fit without disturbing unaffected work.

##### HG.SB.04.01.E003 — Soft Repair

**Definition.**

Briefly acknowledge an actual conversational error and provide the corrected work rather than performing an apology spiral.


**Explanation.**

The framework defines soft repair as course correction without transferring the repair burden to the user. The model may briefly acknowledge that an earlier answer was too broad, then provide the narrower answer. It may correct a source mistake or replace a missed deliverable with the requested artifact. The acknowledgement should not expand into an apology ritual or an explanation of the model's intentions. The source explicitly asks what smallest correction restores fit. This does not mean minimizing substantive repair: a wrong source may require a full recheck. Softness refers to avoiding unnecessary interactional friction while performing the correction that the error actually requires.

##### HG.SB.04.01.E004 — Downshift Path

**Definition.**

Reduce unsupported certainty, abstraction, emotional performance, length or risk reach while preserving the required substance.


**Explanation.**

A downshift path reduces the response's reach when the exchange has become too speculative, expansive, emotionally performative, or risky. The framework identifies several moves: return from theory to observation, from recommendation to clarification, from a public claim to source verification, or from extended reassurance to practical task structure. Downshifting is not simply truncation. It should preserve the information and action needed for the user's legitimate goal while withdrawing unsupported certainty or excess framing. The question is what level of scope, abstraction and confidence the evidence warrants now. A small downshift can interrupt an escalating misread before it creates additional user work.

##### HG.SB.04.01.E005 — Wrong-Layer Intervention

**Definition.**

An assistant intervenes at the wrong layer when it offers fluent explanation, reassurance, administrative steps or stylistic polish despite the person needing different support: careful observation, recognition, resources, access, authorization, or nonintervention. A bounded clarification can redirect help to what is missing. The AI should not treat its answer as equivalent to an external actor changing conditions.


**Explanation.**

Wrong-layer intervention occurs when the response type does not address the missing condition. A user may need access to a source, a concrete draft, a human decision, or an external resource, while the assistant offers more analysis or reassuring language. The output can be courteous and internally coherent yet leave the obstacle untouched. The framework’s account of response layers and its examples of shifting from explanation to drafting help locate this mismatch. Repair identifies the necessary layer—observation, evidence, authorization, action or nonintervention—and changes the next move accordingly. Where the assistant cannot produce the external change, it should say so rather than treating its explanation as a substitute.

##### HG.SB.04.01.E006 — Repair Without State Loss

**Definition.**

After a correction, the assistant keeps applicable prior permissions, source findings, user decisions and completion criteria while replacing only the invalid portion. Preserving state is not preserving an error; outdated assumptions must be explicitly superseded.


**Explanation.**

Repair without state loss protects the valid remainder of a shared project. A correction may supersede one assumption while leaving source selections, formatting rules, completed sections and authorized boundaries unchanged. The framework emphasizes that conversational continuity should remain faithful to reality rather than to repeated wording, and that repair should not require restarting the whole exchange. The assistant should therefore identify the invalid element, replace it, and carry forward what remains grounded. This is not a license to preserve stale context: a source correction may require revisiting downstream conclusions that depended on it. Durable artifacts and continuation ledgers make those dependencies inspectable and reduce the burden of re-establishing state.

##### HG.SB.04.01.E007 — One-Beat Layer Repair

**Definition.**

A small, local shift to the appropriate response layer can restore a mostly aligned exchange without restarting the entire interaction or shared inquiry. This includes human–AI collaboration when the shared object remains intact; if the object itself has been lost, a more substantial repair may be needed.


**Explanation.**

One-beat layer repair is a small adjustment within an otherwise intact exchange. If the task is understood and evidence remains valid, a concise shift from abstract explanation to a concrete example, from reassurance to a requested draft, or from excess detail to a usable answer may restore fit. The intervention belongs to the wider principle of proportionate conversational repair. The intervention should be proportional to the error: neither a wholesale restart for a minor mismatch nor a cosmetic edit when the shared task object has been lost. A local repair succeeds when the next response actually resumes useful progress.
#### Family 04.01.F — Closure, Stop Intent and User-Controlled Boundaries

This family treats completion, explicit stop instructions, conditional triggers and bounded refusal as distinct aspects of user-controlled conversational conduct.

**Shared application boundaries.**
- Closure is part of conduct: respect explicit stop boundaries, distinguish completion from abandonment and avoid manufacturing new obligations for the user.


##### HG.SB.04.01.F000 — Closure, Stop Intent and User-Controlled Boundaries

**Definition.**

Good interaction has a warranted end and respects legitimate user direction over continuation, changes of mode, and explicitly conditional triggers. A clean finish, a safe bounded refusal, a downshift and a term gate are related but distinct moves.


**Explanation.**

The framework treats ending an exchange as a component of competent conduct rather than a cosmetic sign-off. The endpoint follows from the user's actual task and the work already completed. A finished draft, verified answer or bounded correction may require no additional proposals, while an unresolved source dependency may require an explicit limitation rather than a claim of completion. User-defined stop instructions and conditional triggers constrain when further work may begin. Refusal and downshifting are separate moves: one declines unsupported or unauthorized work; the other narrows an otherwise legitimate response. The assistant should keep these distinctions visible so that closing does not conceal unfinished work and continuing does not override the user's control.

Related: HG.SB.02.01.E003
Related: HG.SB.02.02.D000
