Related: HG.SB.02.06.H003
Related: HG.SB.03.02.J007
Related: HG.SB.04.01.I007

##### HG.SB.05.02.C008 — Builders Design / Institutions Execute

**Definition.**

Originating design work and later public administration are separable responsibilities, with transition governed by records and authority rather than private goodwill


**Explanation.**

Builders may define the initial problem, conceptual architecture and intended safeguards. Institutions that later administer the system must carry operational duties: maintaining records, receiving funds, handling review, correcting failures and providing continuity. The framework uses this distinction to explain why good intentions cannot indefinitely substitute for public administration. A builder may remain a valued contributor without retaining final control over every implementation decision. The transition needs versioned design records, an explicit delegation, a method for changing rules and a way to contest departures from purpose. Institutions are not automatically trustworthy merely because they are formal; they must demonstrate the capacity to execute the declared commitments. The analytical boundary is between design authority, actual institutional mandate and verified execution.

Related: HG.SB.02.01.G004
Related: HG.SB.02.06.B006
Related: HG.SB.03.01.B003

##### HG.SB.05.02.C009 — Replaceability as Legitimacy

**Definition.**

A role is credible when scoped records, review and handoff allow its holder to leave, be corrected or be replaced without losing the public function


**Explanation.**

Replaceability tests whether a role has become a dependable institutional function or remains dependent on a particular person. The framework connects it to recorded methods, clear permissions, conflict rules, review, removal and transfer of unfinished work. A reviewer should be replaceable without losing the evidentiary record; an operator without losing service continuity; a registry custodian without losing version history. Replaceability is not a claim that people are interchangeable or disposable. The source explicitly distinguishes human dignity from the consequences attached to roles. Proper transitions preserve contribution and fair treatment while allowing recusal, correction or removal when the public function requires it. An editor should ask what would actually happen after departure, not accept a succession clause as proof of readiness.

Related: HG.SB.02.05.G003

##### HG.SB.05.02.C010 — Nine-Role Stack

**Definition.**

Distinguish rights holder, operator, funder, reviewer, rule evolver, recorder, contributor, beneficiary and exit actor; each may have different permissions and conflicts


The nine roles are an analytic map; a single organization may occupy several roles only with declared safeguards.

**Explanation.**

The nine-role stack is an analytical inventory for locating the parties in a trust relationship. The rights holder controls specified assets or permissions; the operator performs work; the funder supplies resources; the reviewer evaluates claims; the rule evolver changes criteria; the recorder preserves authoritative traces; the contributor adds labor or material; the beneficiary receives intended value; and the exit actor can depart or terminate a relationship under defined conditions. These roles need not correspond to nine organizations. The point is to avoid assuming that contribution implies control, funding implies judgment, or record custody implies the right to alter a result. Where one actor occupies multiple roles, the overlap should be declared and tested for conflict, oversight and practical control. The map is diagnostic, not evidence that separation already exists.

Related: HG.SB.02.06.D003

##### HG.SB.05.02.C012 — No One Allowed to Matter Too Much

**Definition.**

Public reliance should not require any founder, council, mark, operator, expert, platform or metric to become irreplaceable or immune to challenge


**Explanation.**

This principle names the limit on institutional dependence. A founder may offer rare insight, a reviewer may have specialized expertise, and a platform may carry essential records, but public reliance becomes fragile when any one of them cannot be questioned, replaced or bypassed. The framework frames the issue through bounded authority, role separation, refusal rights and replaceability. The test is not whether every person or resource has equal importance; it is whether an indispensable position can escape correction. Design responses may include documented methods, succession, independent record access, appeal, narrow vetoes and a lawful exit route. These are proposed safeguards until implemented and tested. The phrase should not be used to minimize real contributions; it limits unchecked authority while preserving attribution and continuity.
#### Family 05.02.D — Purpose-Bound Money, Receiving Rules and Influence Fences

This family examines how incoming resources become obligations and influence, and how receiving conditions, purpose-bound routing, role separation and records can limit that conversion.

**Shared family guidance.**
- For application, trace the source of funds, purpose, receiving actor, redirect permissions, restrictions, exceptions and records. A conceptual flow diagram is not an executed financial instrument.

##### HG.SB.05.02.D000 — Purpose-Bound Money, Receiving Rules and Influence Fences

**Definition.**

Money and other forms of support create practical relationships of authority and dependence. A governed financial path specifies source, purpose, initial recipient, routing, redirect power, permitted and prohibited influence, records, conflicts and resilience under changes in funding


**Explanation.**

A financial arrangement is part of trust architecture because it determines whose priorities can be acted on and who bears the consequences of scarcity. The framework connects the receiving layer, purpose-bound revenue and money routing to the independence of review and public claims. Analysis begins before funds arrive: identify the giver, recipient, declared use and restrictions. It then follows who can redirect allocations, what record is produced and whether support can purchase authority. Formal conditions must be compared with practical leverage, such as dependence on one sponsor. The resulting map is a design and inspection aid, not proof that a legal instrument exists or that any transaction has occurred. A credible arrangement also states how it responds to shortfalls, changed needs and exit.


Related: HG.SB.02.04.G003

##### HG.SB.05.02.D001 — Money Flow as Human-Grade Design

**Definition.**

Money flow distributes practical influence, obligations and possible burden. Look at source, receiving purpose, redirect rights, conflicts, excluded influence, maintenance responsibilities and correction before treating a funding arrangement as neutral.


**Explanation.**

A budget is not merely an accounting summary when its categories determine which human needs receive attention and which workers absorb unfunded obligations. The framework treats money flow as a design question alongside authority, records and correction. Follow an actual or proposed payment from source to final use, marking who can approve, delay, redirect or refuse it. The analysis should include maintenance costs and the effect of funding loss on promised services. It should also distinguish a permitted consultation right from prohibited influence over standards or independent review. A declared charitable purpose is relevant evidence of intent, but not evidence that money reached the intended work. The operational test is whether the stated allocation, records and consequences agree.


##### HG.SB.05.02.D002 — Purpose-Bound Revenue Architecture

**Definition.**

Received money has an identifiable purpose, permitted uses, recorded paths and specified exceptions before it is treated as discretionary income


**Explanation.**

Purpose-bound revenue makes the relationship between an incoming payment and the institution’s promise explicit. The receiving category identifies what work the payment may finance, which uses are excluded and who may authorize exceptions. The framework emphasizes that a donor’s willingness to support a mission does not itself establish a legitimate right to decide outcomes. The purpose must therefore be separated from any requested influence, publicity or access. A usable architecture records both default routing and approved deviations, allowing later inspection of whether allocations matched their declared objects. Where circumstances require revision, the process for changing the purpose should be identified rather than silently shifting funds. The concept describes a governance discipline; implementation depends on appropriate legal, financial and operational arrangements.


##### HG.SB.05.02.D003 — Mechanical Money Spine

**Definition.**

Precommitted purposes and recorded exceptions constrain arbitrary movement of funds among care, commons maintenance, paid construction and other obligations. A category diagram does not prove that allocations are honored.


A default routing diagram must be compared with actual transactions and governed exceptions.

**Explanation.**

The mechanical money spine is the default route that limits opportunistic redirection after funds have been received. The framework describes precommitted pathways as a protection against pressure from funders, founders, operators and immediate institutional convenience. Mechanical does not mean that no judgment is possible: it means a deviation must be authorized, justified and recorded. Separate categories for care, commons maintenance, builder compensation and other legitimate functions make conflicting purposes visible. The analytic task is to compare the stated route with transaction records, restrictions and exceptions, including who approved any change. A polished flowchart without actual receiving controls, records or enforceable permissions is only a proposal. Privacy-appropriate evidence can establish whether routing was followed without publishing sensitive beneficiary details.


##### HG.SB.05.02.D004 — Receiving Layer Discipline

**Definition.**

Accept support only after identifying sender, purpose, obligations, association, excluded influence, record and refusal conditions


**Explanation.**

The receiving layer governs what enters the system before it becomes an unexamined source of leverage. The framework extends this principle beyond money to labor, data, partnerships, visibility and legitimacy, but financial receipt provides a concrete test. The recipient should know who is offering support, what it is for, which obligations follow, what association may be publicly claimed and what authority is explicitly excluded. A refusal path is essential when an offer conflicts with these boundaries. Records should identify accepted terms without exposing unnecessary private information. The distinction matters because a gift can generate expectations even without a formal vote or ownership interest. Clear receipt conditions protect both sides by making the terms inspectable before reliance grows.

##### HG.SB.05.02.D005 — Money Purpose Before Arrival

**Definition.**

Determine whether funds support care, operation, review, public claims or other purposes before acceptance creates implicit obligations


**Explanation.**

Pre-acceptance classification reduces the risk that a later urgent need or a donor’s expectations will redefine a payment’s purpose. The framework argues that money becomes influence where receiving rules remain ambiguous. An institution should therefore identify whether an offered sum supports care, common infrastructure, operating capacity, independent review or another defined function. Each category carries different permissions, conflicts and record needs. Review funding, for example, must not be treated as a purchase of favorable findings. An ambiguous offer can be clarified, limited or declined rather than absorbed into general discretionary funds. This is a sequencing rule, not a claim that every allocation can be permanently fixed. Legitimate changes require identified authority and a recorded exception or amendment.


##### HG.SB.05.02.D006 — Capital as Fuel, Not Control

**Definition.**

Investment or donation may finance legitimate work without buying standards, review outcomes, data access or general governance powers


Capital can support operations without purchasing criteria, independent review or public status.

**Explanation.**

Capital can enable a system to operate while also exposing it to pressure from those able to withdraw or increase support. The framework frames this as a boundary between financing work and controlling the trust claim. A funder may receive negotiated information or participation rights, but those rights should be named and separated from independent judgment, confidential data and standards revision. The inspection should cover both contractual permissions and informal dependence: an actor may influence decisions through anticipated future funding even without a formal vote. The principle does not deny that investors or donors can have legitimate rights; it requires that those rights be scoped and disclosed. Funding arrangements are credible when they preserve the decision and review boundaries the public is asked to rely upon.


##### HG.SB.05.02.D007 — Informal Money-to-Influence Conversion

**Definition.**

Anticipated donor, client or platform reactions can shape decisions without formal votes or ownership rights


**Explanation.**

Influence can travel through expectations rather than explicit instructions. An operator may hesitate to publish an unfavorable finding, change a criterion or reject a partnership because a major supporter might leave. The framework treats this dependence as relevant to anti-capture design even when governance documents assign no formal authority to the supporter. Inspection therefore asks who supplies essential resources, which decisions are sensitive to withdrawal and whether independent actors have practical capacity to refuse. A conflict register or formal firewall may help but cannot alone prove independence. Evidence should distinguish observed interference, credible structural exposure and hypothetical concern. The appropriate response is to make incentives and corrective options visible, not to assume every donor or client is acting improperly.


##### HG.SB.05.02.D008 — Governance Before Money; Money Before Influence

**Definition.**

Specify governance, conflicts and refusal boundaries before significant funding arrives; distinguish declared legitimate influence from covert decision purchase


**Explanation.**

Sequence matters because an institution that accepts major support before defining its decision rights may later struggle to reject the influence attached to it. The framework places receiving discipline and purpose-bound routing upstream of public trust claims. Before acceptance, the system should identify permitted uses, conflict disclosures, review independence, refusal holders and any authorized role for the supporter. After acceptance, actual transfers and decisions can be checked against those conditions. The phrase does not prohibit negotiated influence categorically: some governance or consultation rights may be legitimate if explicit and appropriately bounded. The concern is an undisclosed conversion of financial dependence into control over standards, status or public interpretation. Written rules require corresponding decision capacity and records to be operative.


Related: HG.SB.02.03.C003
Related: HG.SB.02.06.G005

##### HG.SB.05.02.D009 — Money-Flow Role Overlay

**Definition.**

Map giver, receiver, purpose-setter, mover, redirector, veto holder, record keeper and bearer of loss, including informal money power


**Explanation.**

A single financial transaction may involve several distinct authorities that an organization chart compresses into one title. The role overlay asks who gives, receives, classifies, moves, redirects, blocks and records money, and who suffers if it is unavailable or misused. The framework uses such separation to reveal where nominally independent functions are effectively controlled by one actor. The map should distinguish legal permission from actual access to accounts and practical capacity to delay payments. It should also show where a refusal can be reviewed and where an exception is recorded. The bearer of loss matters because financial discretion can shift costs onto beneficiaries, workers or public infrastructure. This overlay is a diagnostic representation; only verified permissions and transactions establish what actually happens.


##### HG.SB.05.02.D010 — Scenario-Resilient Money Design

**Definition.**

Test how money purposes and oversight survive growth, loss of support, changed needs, actor exit, capture pressure and responsible shutdown


**Explanation.**

A routing scheme that works only while one founder, donor or operator remains cooperative is fragile. The framework calls for pressure-testing money purposes against growth, withdrawal of funding, changed beneficiaries, institutional capture and orderly exit. Scenarios can ask who may revise allocations, how restricted funds are handled, whether maintenance obligations continue and which records survive a shutdown. They can also expose dependence on an irreplaceable payment approver or private custodian. A good test states the assumed conditions and the proposed response, including the authorized decision holder and evidence required. It should not be reported as a demonstrated stress result unless the system has actually been exercised and inspected. Resilience is a claim requiring operational evidence, not a property bestowed by a scenario table.


##### HG.SB.05.02.D011 — Financial Intent versus Financial Routing

**Definition.**

A benevolent allocation intention differs from enforceable receiving categories, redirect permissions, records and actual transfers


Benevolent financial intent does not demonstrate controlled receipt, routing or disbursement.

**Explanation.**

A promise to direct money toward a good purpose is not the same as a controlled financial route. The framework distinguishes the moral appeal of a funding story from the structure that determines what can be received, moved and corrected. Analysis should identify the recipient account or institution, the category attached to the funds, the authority to change it, the evidence of transfer and the review path when a mismatch appears. A proposal, diagram or public statement may establish intended design but not completed disbursement. Conversely, a verified transfer establishes movement, not necessarily the full downstream benefit claimed. This distinction protects against both unwarranted reassurance and excessive suspicion: assess each level of evidence according to what it actually demonstrates.
#### Family 05.02.E — Care, Commons and Builder Resource Stewardship

This family distinguishes direct care commitments, shared infrastructure maintenance and compensated builder labor as separate but compatible resource purposes.

**Shared family guidance.**
- For application, identify the designated beneficiary, permissible use, oversight, privacy protection and maintenance obligations. Do not treat care, commons and builder support as interchangeable accounts.

##### HG.SB.05.02.E000 — Care, Commons and Builder Resource Stewardship

**Definition.**

Care support, maintenance of shared infrastructure, and compensation of people who build or steward systems can legitimately coexist but have different promised beneficiaries, authority, records, risks and timing. These purposes should not be silently converted into one another


**Explanation.**

The three resource purposes make different promises to different parties. Care concerns support reaching intended people or care-enabling work; commons funding concerns shared infrastructure that remains usable; builder support concerns the labor and continuity required to sustain either. The framework describes these as distinct channels within purpose-bound money design, not a hierarchy in which one is inherently illegitimate. The editorial task is to name the beneficiary, authorized expenses, decision rights and relevant records for each channel. A shared budget may be administratively convenient, but convenience cannot silently change a care commitment into operating revenue or an unpaid maintenance burden. Distinguish the design of an allocation from evidence of actual disbursement. Where a purpose needs revision, identify the authorized change process and the consequences for prior promises.


Related: HG.SB.01.03.F007
Related: HG.SB.02.05.G006

##### HG.SB.05.02.E001 — Care Money Is for Care

**Definition.**

Care-designated resources should reach specified care or care-enabling activities rather than silently finance unrelated visibility, prestige or growth


Care-related operational costs require explicit definition and disclosure rather than silent absorption.

**Explanation.**

Care-designated money carries a narrower reliance claim than general institutional support: the contributor or public is told that resources will reach a particular care purpose. The framework treats diversion into prestige, growth or unrelated operations as a mismatch between the public-facing promise and the financial path. This does not mean all administration is forbidden. Intake, safeguarding, coordination or delivery may be genuine care-enabling costs when defined within the commitment and disclosed appropriately. Inspection should identify the promised purpose, permissible direct and indirect expenses, authorizer of exceptions, and records showing allocation and delivery. If money is rerouted, a new explanation alone does not erase the original obligation. The operative issue is whether actual use remains consistent with the care claim or has been transparently and legitimately changed.


##### HG.SB.05.02.E002 — Care Flow Independence

**Definition.**

Care eligibility and allocation should not depend on a recipient's publicity value or on donor/brand preferences outside declared conditions


**Explanation.**

A care pathway can be distorted even when resources formally remain in a care account. The framework identifies donor preferences, reputational protection, branding and product retention as possible pressures on who receives assistance and when. The test is whether eligibility and allocation follow declared care criteria rather than the recipient’s usefulness to the institution’s image. A donor may legitimately restrict a gift to a stated program or population; the concern arises when undisclosed influence overrides the represented basis of need or access. Inspect decision criteria, exception authority, conflicts, refusal routes and records suited to the sensitivity of recipients. Privacy should prevent publicity demands from becoming a condition of support. The concept diagnoses a governance vulnerability; it does not establish that a particular donor or operator has acted improperly.


##### HG.SB.05.02.E003 — Care / Commons / Builder Time

**Definition.**

Direct support, shared infrastructure and compensated maintenance or creation are distinct legitimate resource purposes that must be inspectable in context


**Explanation.**

The three-part distinction prevents a broad public-good label from concealing incompatible uses. Care may involve direct assistance or activities required to deliver it. Commons work maintains archives, tools, access and other shared capabilities. Builder time compensates the people who construct, review or maintain those capabilities. Each category has a different time horizon, beneficiary and failure mode: immediate unmet need, infrastructure decay or unsustainable labor. A design should state which costs belong to which purpose and how shared expenses are apportioned. Reviewers can then examine whether an apparently generous care program depends on unpaid maintainers, or whether a commons allocation quietly replaces promised direct support. These are analytic resource categories, not proof of separate bank accounts or completed transfers.


##### HG.SB.05.02.E004 — Builder Stake as Stabilizer

**Definition.**

Bounded compensation and security for maintainers can protect mission continuity without granting unlimited private extraction or ownership


**Explanation.**

The framework argues that expecting permanent sacrifice from builders can create fragility, burnout and dependence on powerful funders. Stable compensation and predictable maintenance capacity can therefore protect a public-purpose mission rather than contradict it. The stabilizing role depends on limits: payment for work does not confer indefinite authority over standards, public records or beneficiaries. Inspection should distinguish wages, fees, reserves and agreed participation rights from ownership or veto powers. It should also ask whether the system can replace a departing maintainer without losing access to essential records or infrastructure. Excessive private extraction is one failure; uncompensated dependence is another. The relevant question is whether the arrangement sustains competent human work while keeping its authority bounded, recorded and reviewable.


##### HG.SB.05.02.E005 — Operations as Infrastructure, Not Profit

**Definition.**

Pay for real hosting, record keeping, support, review and repair without designing operational charges to reward dependence or delayed correction


**Explanation.**

Operations are necessary to keep a public-purpose promise usable: hosting, security, records, assistance, independent review and repair all consume resources. The framework cautions that this operational layer can become a hidden profit center if revenue improves when users remain confused, dependent or unable to finish. The appropriate distinction is between justified compensation for infrastructure and incentives that reward avoidable friction. Examine what operational charges purchase, how they are approved, whether unresolved cases generate recurring fees and whether maintenance is adequately funded. A service may need reserves and paid staff without making accumulation its mission. Evidence requires budgets, contracts, operating practices and outcome records; a statement that operations are nonprofit or mission-driven is not enough to establish the actual incentive structure.


##### HG.SB.05.02.E006 — Circulation, Not Accumulation

**Definition.**

Legitimate reserves and surplus differ from wealth retention as an independent institutional end; review where value is routed and who can redirect it


**Explanation.**

Circulation asks what resources enable after they enter the system. The framework distinguishes sustaining reserves and legitimate surplus from treating retained wealth or institutional expansion as a self-justifying objective. A prudent reserve may protect continuity during funding interruptions; the same label can also obscure indefinite diversion from declared beneficiaries if its purpose, cap or governance is undefined. Follow the allocation rules for incoming revenue, surplus, reserve use and exceptional transfers. Identify who can authorize redirection and whether the public-facing purpose remains accurate after changes. The test is not whether every dollar is spent immediately, but whether retention and movement of value remain answerable to specified care, commons and maintenance obligations. Actual transaction evidence is needed to judge practice.


##### HG.SB.05.02.E007 — Care Allocation Privacy

**Definition.**

Public accountability can be maintained through suitable records and review without exposing those receiving assistance


Privacy protection and financial accountability can coexist through restricted or aggregated records.

**Explanation.**

Care funding creates a dual obligation: demonstrate that resources followed their declared purpose while protecting people whose circumstances may be sensitive. The framework’s trust architecture does not equate inspectability with publishing personal case details. Suitable mechanisms can include restricted case records, aggregated expenditure categories, independent review and documented eligibility procedures, depending on the context and governing requirements. The audience should be able to understand what was promised, what type of support was delivered and how errors can be challenged without gaining unnecessary access to identities or vulnerabilities. Avoid using privacy as a blanket excuse for unreviewable allocations, but also avoid making public exposure a condition of receiving care. A proposed privacy design is not itself evidence that access controls or audits operate.


##### HG.SB.05.02.E008 — Commons Maintenance versus Care Delivery

**Definition.**

Funding shared public tools and supporting particular people are different duties; underfunding either one may transfer burdens to users or workers


**Explanation.**

Shared tools and direct care have different cost structures. A public archive or service interface may require long-term hosting, updates, security and human support, while a care allocation may be committed to particular recipients or interventions. The framework treats both as legitimate public-good functions but warns against silently exchanging one obligation for the other. Underfunded maintenance can leave users with inaccessible services and workers with uncompensated repair labor. Underfunded care can leave an impressive infrastructure without the promised assistance. The editorial test identifies both delivery and upkeep commitments, their decision holders, expected duration and evidence of fulfillment. A single headline total for public-benefit spending can conceal these distinctions. Neither a maintenance plan nor a care pledge establishes that the corresponding work occurred.


##### HG.SB.05.02.E009 — Builder Compensation versus Contributor Control

**Definition.**

Compensation for labor is not itself an ownership claim or permission to override public-purpose governance


**Explanation.**

Paying contributors and maintainers recognizes real work; it does not by itself transfer the right to set standards, control public status or override beneficiary protections. The framework pairs builder stability with contribution-without-control and role-bounded authority. This distinction protects both sides: the institution should not exploit contributors by invoking the commons, and contributors should not turn compensation or authorship into an undisclosed governing mandate. Review agreements for the work compensated, intellectual-property or participation rights actually granted, conflict restrictions, decision authority and handoff duties. A contributor may have negotiated governance rights, but those rights must be explicit and accountable rather than presumed from labor performed. The relevant evidence is the operative arrangement and practice, not the moral prestige of contribution.
#### Family 05.02.F — Commons, Non-Extractive Operation and Public-Good Durability

This family examines mission-bound public-good operation, commons obligations, sustainable funding, maintenance, bounded assessments and responsible exit.

**Shared family guidance.**
- For application, inspect access, operating costs, data capture, user dependency, human compensation, maintenance and exit. Public-benefit language is not evidence that extraction is absent.

##### HG.SB.05.02.F000 — Commons, Non-Extractive Operation and Public-Good Durability

**Definition.**

A claimed public-good operator is evaluated by who gains value and power, who bears burden, whether common tools and human workers remain supported, and whether users have meaningful control, completion and exit. Non-extractive arrangements require specific evidence and adaptation, not virtue words


**Explanation.**

The public-good claim describes a relationship among users, maintainers, resources and institutional power, not a favorable organizational identity. The framework asks whether a tool reduces shared burden, supports completion and exit, protects information and remains maintained without making public reliance dependent on private discretion. A review should therefore follow actual value and authority: who benefits, who supplies labor, what data is collected, what funding conditions constrain decisions and what happens when a user leaves. A nonprofit label or free interface cannot by itself settle these questions. Durability also matters: a tool that lacks repair, security or retirement capacity may eventually transfer costs to users and workers. Any conclusion about non-extraction should identify its scope, date and evidence, and remain open to correction as the operator changes.


Related: HG.SB.01.01.C004

##### HG.SB.05.02.F001 — Non-Extractive Operators and Commons Funding

**Definition.**

A public-purpose operator must sustain access, care, shared tools and maintainers without covertly relying on users' data, dependency or contributors' power for private capture


**Explanation.**

The operator needs resources to keep its commitments, but a survival mechanism can contradict those commitments. The framework treats maintenance, fair labor, accessible service and legitimate reserves as real needs, while warning against financing them through hidden data capture, artificial dependence or privileged control purchased by contributors. Inspect the relationship between operating costs and revenue: whether a fee is disclosed, whether funding buys review outcomes, whether user information is repurposed and whether contributors receive fair treatment without acquiring unbounded governance rights. A viable design can combine multiple sources of support, provided each has clear limits and records. The distinction is between transparent support for a public function and extracting value from the very reliance that the public function promises to protect.


##### HG.SB.05.02.F002 — Commons Tool Contract

**Definition.**

A shared tool entails explicit duties for purpose, access, upkeep, privacy, contributions, funding, records, exit and retirement. This is a conceptual obligation structure, not an executed agreement or claim of legal sufficiency.


A commons tool contract here is a conceptual obligations map, not a legally operative contract.

**Explanation.**

A commons tool should not be described as shared solely because many people can use it. The framework asks who maintains it, what access is promised, what information is retained, how contributors participate, how problems are reported and how the tool can be retired responsibly. The conceptual contract gathers these obligations into an inspectable map: purpose and intended users; permitted and excluded uses; stewardship and funding; update, correction and record duties; contribution rights; and meaningful exit. Its value is diagnostic. It can reveal an unassigned maintainer, a missing privacy boundary or an indefinite service promise that available resources cannot honor. It does not create enforceable rights by being written, establish legal compliance or prove the named duties are being performed. Those require separate institutional, operational and, where appropriate, legal validation.


##### HG.SB.05.02.F003 — Mission-Locked Operator

**Definition.**

Bind an operator's practical decisions on money, data, product, claims and transfer to declared purpose while allowing accountable adaptation of methods


**Explanation.**

The framework defines mission lock through the authority an operator actually exercises. It may constrain revenue routing, data use, product incentives, public claims, rule changes, transfer and record custody. The point is not to freeze every workflow; methods may need revision as users, costs or risks change. Instead, the declared purpose supplies boundaries for permissible adaptation and for challenge when a decision drifts outside them. Review should identify the decision holder, the action requiring approval, any refusal or independent review right, the relevant record and the consequence of breach. Organizational form alone does not establish a mission lock: a nonprofit, open-source project or public body can still exercise unchecked discretion. Conversely, different legal forms may support bounded operation if the operative constraints can be demonstrated.


Related: HG.SB.02.06.I001
Related: HG.SB.03.01.F005
Related: HG.SB.03.03.D004

##### HG.SB.05.02.F004 — Non-Extractive Eligibility Test

**Definition.**

Examine actual value flows, data, dependence, maintenance, contribution, surplus and exit before making a bounded, dated assessment of a non-extraction claim


**Explanation.**

Eligibility is a scoped evaluation rather than an enduring virtue designation. The framework directs attention to where value flows, whether users can finish and leave, what data is taken, how workers and contributors are treated, and whether shared infrastructure receives adequate maintenance. The reviewer should specify the service version, time period, evidence available and unresolved questions. A product might avoid advertising extraction yet still rely on underpaid labor; another might charge an explicit maintenance fee while preserving autonomy and exit. Neither pricing alone nor public-benefit language answers the question. A positive assessment should therefore name the particular practices supported by records, the exclusions from review and conditions that would trigger reconsideration. It must not be generalized into certification of an entire organization without corresponding evidence and authority.


##### HG.SB.05.02.F005 — Commons Funding

**Definition.**

Shared infrastructure, archives, care resources and public-good tools require sustainable maintenance, access, security and human work. Funding must not quietly become extractive control or impose permanent unpaid sacrifice on builders and users. Make costs, funding conditions and influence boundaries inspectable.


**Explanation.**

Commons funding addresses the continuing work after a tool or archive is launched. The framework identifies upkeep, security, documentation, accessible service, correction and paid human attention as legitimate resource demands. Treating all this labor as voluntary can conceal a transfer of institutional cost onto builders and users. Yet accepting funds without limits may let donors, clients or platforms influence access, criteria, public status or data use. A funding design should state the maintained asset, recurring obligations, funding source, receiving authority, permitted influence, records and fallback when support declines. The same analysis should include reserves and responsible retirement rather than indefinite availability promises. The claim of sustainability remains provisional until actual costs, disbursements, maintenance and governance are observed.


##### HG.SB.05.02.F007 — One-Tree Infrastructure

**Definition.**

Source metaphor for diverse autonomous public functions sharing a maintained foundation of purposes, records, resources and accountability without one unchecked owner


**Explanation.**

The one-tree image illustrates a shared root of mission and trust architecture with distinct branches for care, learning, tools, review and other public functions. It is not an instruction to centralize every decision in one organization. Different branches may need different records, access rules, funding and review authorities, while benefiting from common purpose and maintained infrastructure. The metaphor is useful when fragmented programs forget the costs or commitments they share, or when a successful branch begins to treat common resources as its private asset. Translate the image into explicit allocations: what is shared, what remains autonomous, who maintains the root, who can redirect resources and how disputes are reviewed. Without those details, the tree remains a teaching image rather than evidence of functioning governance.


##### HG.SB.05.02.F008 — Public-Good Engine for Non-Extractive Tools

**Definition.**

Combine mission constraint, purpose funding, paid maintenance, limited data capture, contribution limits, scope, records and exit into a coherent public-purpose arrangement


**Explanation.**

A non-extractive public-good tool needs its components to reinforce rather than defeat one another. The framework links mission-bound operation, controlled funding, compensation, privacy, contribution without control, honest claims and user exit. A system may publish a strong mission while designing revenue around endless engagement, or protect user data while relying on unmaintained infrastructure. The engine concept prompts a whole-system inspection of such contradictions. For a particular tool, map its intended done-state, funding and maintenance requirements, information flows, decision rights, public claims, correction routes and shutdown plan. Record where these mechanisms are merely proposed and where they operate. Coherence is the goal: no single positive feature establishes that the complete arrangement is non-extractive or durable.


##### HG.SB.05.02.F010 — Operator Survival Without Extraction

**Definition.**

If genuine maintenance cannot be funded without contradicting public commitments, narrow the service, seek different support, transfer, pause or retire it openly


Responsible narrowing or retirement may better preserve purpose than unfunded promises.

**Explanation.**

The framework treats survival as a real constraint rather than a moral embarrassment: people require pay, infrastructure requires upkeep and review requires capacity. The danger appears when the operator uses survival to justify harvesting more data, trapping users, selling trust status or quietly abandoning service obligations. The relevant choice is not simply growth or collapse. An operator can reduce scope, adjust disclosed funding, transfer stewardship, suspend unsafe functions or retire the service with appropriate notice and records. Each option has consequences for users and maintainers that should be evaluated explicitly. The public claim should contract when the capacity to honor it contracts. A responsible exit is therefore part of trustworthy operation, not proof that the original mission lacked value.


##### HG.SB.05.02.F011 — Humane Paths Made Easier Than Extraction

**Definition.**

Structure ordinary funding, staffing and product choices so useful completion, care and shared maintenance are easier than profitable confusion or dependence


**Explanation.**

The framework closes by asking whether the ordinary institutional path rewards humane conduct. Product metrics, funding incentives and staffing decisions can otherwise make user confusion, extended dependence or exaggerated claims financially attractive. The design response is concrete: reward completed tasks and clean exit, fund maintenance directly, compensate care and review work, limit data collection, and keep public status separate from purchasing power. Review should examine the default decision paths, not only exceptional statements of values. Who gains when a user finishes? What happens to revenue when a complaint is resolved? Is correction funded and authorized? These questions reveal whether humane behavior is structurally easier. The principle does not predict that every actor will behave well; it asks institutions to reduce the routine incentives to betray their declared purpose.

#### Family 05.02.G — Institutional Capture, Concentration and Incentive Drift

This family distinguishes institutional capture pathways and tests effective authority against formal arrangements.

**Shared family guidance.**
- For application, trace the concrete concentration of money, status, operational access, review or records, and the available correction mechanism. Structural risk alone does not establish malign intent.

##### HG.SB.05.02.G000 — Institutional Capture, Concentration and Incentive Drift

**Definition.**

Founding goodwill and well-described roles can fail when authority, resources, review, public status or practical access converge into uncorrectable power. Identify the particular capture pathway, evidence and possibility of correction without presuming bad motives from structural overlap alone


**Explanation.**

Institutional capture is a failure of effective limits, not simply a judgment about character. The framework asks who can decide, who controls money and records, who reviews a claim, and whether an affected party can obtain a consequential correction. A system may display separated titles while a single actor controls the infrastructure or relationships on which the others depend. Examine the pathway: a funding condition, exclusive data access, appointment power, symbolic authority or an unusable refusal right. Then distinguish a plausible vulnerability from documented exercise of control. Corrective design may require independent review, narrower permissions, durable records, enforceable recusals or transferable operations. A capture diagnosis should specify evidence, actual consequences and unresolved questions rather than treating concentrated roles as proof of intent.

##### HG.SB.05.02.G001 — Sincerity Does Not Scale by Itself

**Definition.**

Growing money, dependence, status and disagreement can outlast personal good intentions; public duties need independent structures


**Explanation.**

The framework treats sincerity as valuable but structurally insufficient. Early collaborators can coordinate through shared memory and personal restraint, yet growth adds funders, successors, users and conflicting expectations. A promise that works because one person is trusted becomes fragile when that person is unavailable or disagrees with a reviewer. Translate good intentions into explicit decision rights, purpose restrictions, records, conflict handling and review routes. The test is not whether founders are sincere; it is whether people who do not share their history can inspect and challenge an action without appealing to personal goodwill. Scaling therefore requires accountable procedures that survive changes of personnel, money and public attention. It does not require presuming dishonesty in the original group.

##### HG.SB.05.02.G002 — Trust Should Not Depend on Private Sincerity

**Definition.**

A trusted founding circle's private expectations cannot substitute for public roles, inspectable limits and correction after personnel change


**Explanation.**

Private restraint cannot be reliably audited by a person outside the founding circle. The framework distinguishes a good actor from a good authority arrangement: the former may be conscientious, while the latter states what decisions are allowed and what happens after error. Inspect whether standards are written, whether money can be redirected, whether review findings can be overturned without explanation and whether the record survives departure. The point is to make bounded trust possible without asking the public to infer motives. A new reviewer should be able to find a mandate and correction route rather than reconstruct unwritten understandings. Sincerity can support the structure, but cannot replace independent constraints or make an unrecorded decision publicly answerable.

##### HG.SB.05.02.G003 — Anti-Capture Failure Mode Taxonomy

**Definition.**

Distinguish founder, funder, operator, council, symbol, commons and soft capture rather than assuming one generic institutional corruption pathway


**Explanation.**

The taxonomy separates different routes through which public-purpose institutions can lose effective accountability. Founder capture centers on origin and interpretation; funder capture on resource dependence; operator capture on operational access; council capture on compromised judgment; symbol capture on public reputation outrunning the mechanism; commons capture on shared resources redirected to private ends; and soft capture on deference and avoidance of consequences. The framework treats these as diagnostic distinctions rather than allegations about any named organization. Each route requires its own evidence and remedy. For example, disclosing a donation does not fix exclusive operator access, while replacing an operator may not restore independent review. A useful assessment maps the specific authority or dependency and tests whether an affected party can secure correction.

##### HG.SB.05.02.G004 — Founder Capture

**Definition.**

Originator memory, symbolic status or informal veto becomes the only permissible interpretation or route to institutional correction


Founder capture may emerge from others’ deference even without the founder seeking control.

**Explanation.**

An originator may retain indispensable knowledge or become the public face of a system without intending to monopolize it. Capture risk emerges when interpretation of purpose, appointment, funding or correction effectively requires that person’s assent. The framework separates founder authorship from continuing institutional authority and asks whether the public function survives the founder leaving the room. Inspect both formal powers and informal deference: can a reviewer disagree, can a successor access records, and can a decision be changed through an authorized process? Safeguards include documented criteria, bounded advisory roles, independent judgment and genuine handoff. A founder’s prominence is not itself evidence of misconduct; the relevant question is whether it prevents accountable disagreement or replacement.

Related: HG.SB.01.03.A004
Related: HG.SB.02.05.A000

##### HG.SB.05.02.G005 — Funder Capture

**Definition.**

Money or anticipated funder preferences alter rulemaking, status or review beyond declared support rights


**Explanation.**

Funder capture may occur through contractual powers or through an organization’s anticipation of what a donor will tolerate. The framework treats money as a practical authority pathway: who receives it, what purpose binds it, who may redirect it and which decisions the funder cannot purchase. Review whether standards, public claims, appointments or adverse findings shift when support is threatened. Legitimate consultation and negotiated reporting rights should be distinguished from covert control over independent judgment. Evidence might include changed criteria, suppressed records or undocumented exceptions, not merely the presence of a large donation. A remedy may involve diversified support, purpose restrictions, conflict disclosure, independent review and recorded refusal rights that remain usable under financial pressure.

##### HG.SB.05.02.G006 — Operator Capture

**Definition.**

Day-to-day infrastructure or information control makes an operator effectively unreviewable despite separated formal titles


**Explanation.**

A board or council may formally govern while the operator controls the databases, credentials, communications and practical means of implementing decisions. The framework directs attention to real control rather than organizational diagrams. Ask who can retrieve a complete record, execute a correction, suspend an unsupported claim, move the service or authorize a handoff. If independent reviewers cannot verify facts or implement consequences without the operator’s cooperation, separation may be nominal. Countermeasures can include access protocols, audit trails, independent record custody, service continuity plans and replaceable operating contracts. Operational concentration may be justified temporarily by scale or expertise; assess whether its scope is declared, monitored and correctable before describing it as capture.

##### HG.SB.05.02.G007 — Council or Review Capture

**Definition.**

A supposedly independent judgment body becomes decorative, dependent, conflict-bound or immune to correction


A council can be captured through dependence or through unreviewable overreach; both require separate evidence.

**Explanation.**

A review body can lose independence in opposite ways. It may become ceremonial, unable to obtain records or impose a consequence; alternatively, it may accumulate unbounded discretion and escape review itself. The framework emphasizes scoped authority, documented reasons, conflict controls and a path to correct mistaken judgments. Examine appointment and removal rules, financing, access to evidence, recusals and whether the council can refuse an unsupported status. Then ask who can challenge a council error without nullifying its legitimate independence. A prestigious roster is not proof of authority, and an unpopular decision is not proof of capture. The diagnosis must identify the specific dependency or unreviewable power and the operational change required.

##### HG.SB.05.02.G008 — Commons Capture

**Definition.**

Tools or shared resources justified by public benefit redirect attention, records or benefits toward private control


**Explanation.**

A commons may be publicly described as shared while decisions about access, data, maintenance and surplus become privately controlled. The framework ties public-good claims to the actual allocation of benefits and burdens. Trace who can change licensing or access terms, move assets, monetize user information, discontinue maintenance or prevent contributors from exiting. A free tool is not automatically a protected commons, and payment to maintainers is not automatically extraction. The key distinction is whether stewardship remains purpose-bound and reviewable. Appropriate safeguards may include transparent operating costs, bounded contributor rights, independent records, data limits and transfer or retirement procedures. Assess actual flows and permissions before concluding that a common resource has been captured.

##### HG.SB.05.02.G009 — Soft Capture / Refusal Without Force

**Definition.**

No explicit power grab is necessary when reputation, gratitude, missing vetoes and practical dependencies make objection ineffective


**Explanation.**

Soft capture arises when nobody must formally order compliance because participants feel unable to object. The framework describes how community goodwill, reputation, gratitude and avoidance of conflict can displace consequences, leaving persistent or powerful actors with practical control. Look for complaints that cannot alter decisions, refusal rights that exist only on paper, or reviewers who avoid recording adverse findings to preserve relationships. This mechanism differs from overt coercion and does not establish malicious intent. Its remedy is not greater suspicion alone: give affected roles usable refusal and escalation paths, protect dissent, document decisions and attach consequences to justified challenges. A supportive culture becomes more credible when disagreement can produce a bounded, reviewable change.

Related: HG.SB.02.06.G005

##### HG.SB.05.02.G010 — Governance Appearance versus Effective Power

**Definition.**

A polished chart, trusted founder or published map may conceal unrecorded decision rights, weak vetoes or missing consequences; inspect actual authority before alleging intent


**Explanation.**

Governance documents are representations of authority, not the authority itself. The framework repeatedly distinguishes a designed arrangement from an operating institution: a chart can name a reviewer without giving access to records, or depict a veto that cannot halt a transaction. Test a consequential decision end to end. Who proposes it, who may approve or refuse, what evidence is available, who records the outcome and what changes after a successful challenge? Compare stated procedures with observed practice and identify any gap precisely. A gap can reflect immature implementation, resource shortage or conflicting mandates; it does not by itself prove deception. The useful result is a concrete repair requirement, not a generalized verdict about the people involved.


Related: HG.SB.02.01.G004
Related: HG.SB.02.05.C006
#### Family 05.02.H — Governance Repair, Shock Resilience and Responsible Evolution

This family examines how institutions report failure, repair instruments, survive role and funding shocks, and preserve public duties through accountable transitions.

**Shared family guidance.**
- For application, name the failure or shock, the responsible actor, decision authority, record, immediate protection, repair route and later review. A plan is not evidence that a repair occurred.

##### HG.SB.05.02.H000 — Governance Repair, Shock Resilience and Responsible Evolution

**Definition.**

A credible institution anticipates failure, succession, scarcity, growth, disputed decisions and instrument drift through specific response, correction and transition paths. Repair changes the affected structures without abandoning purpose or turning an early teaching design into authoritative deployment


**Explanation.**

Governance repair begins with a named failure and a defined response, not an assurance that an institution will adapt. The framework connects trust claims to action, records, review, and consequences; its failure and instrument-repair discussions show why procedures must remain correctable as conditions change. For a funding interruption, contested decision or failing registry, identify who may pause the affected activity, protect those relying on it, preserve relevant records, and authorize a change. Distinguish immediate containment from a durable revision and subsequent independent review. A revised process should preserve the underlying public purpose while disclosing changed permissions, scope and status. An exercise or governance diagram can expose gaps in readiness, but cannot establish that any organization has implemented these controls or successfully repaired a real failure.

Related: HG.SB.03.01.B003
Related: HG.SB.04.01.G009

##### HG.SB.05.02.H001 — Failure Without Shame

**Definition.**

Permit proportionate, protected failure reporting while retaining records, protection against retaliation, correction and consequences for actual harm


**Explanation.**

The framework explicitly treats failure without shame as a condition for reportable, correctable and learnable institutional practice. Humiliation can encourage operators to conceal mistakes, reviewers to soften findings, and affected people to avoid reporting. The alternative is not immunity from accountability. A useful process protects the reporting channel, preserves an accurate account of what occurred, determines immediate safeguards, and specifies proportionate consequences and possible restoration. Privacy and protection against retaliation should be designed alongside review, rather than achieved by erasing the record. Public notice should communicate what others need to know without making spectacle the remedy. Examine whether a person can raise a concern without losing access or standing, and whether the organization can demonstrate what changed afterward. A written reporting policy alone is not proof that reporting is safe.

Related: HG.SB.02.06.G002
Related: HG.SB.03.01.F005
Related: HG.SB.03.04.E010

##### HG.SB.05.02.H002 — Instrument Repair as Principle Maintenance

**Definition.**

When a registry, rubric, veto map or scoreboard becomes burdensome or gameable, revise the instrument while preserving its public-purpose duties


A broken instrument can be repaired without discarding the public purpose it was designed to serve.

**Explanation.**

The framework identifies registries, scoreboards, rubrics, maps and status systems as instruments that may drift from their intended work. A registry can become too costly to maintain; a score can reward gaming; a veto map may describe protections no one can exercise. Repair requires identifying the duty the instrument was meant to discharge before changing its form. Specify the failure, users affected, retained records, proposed revision, decision authority and test for whether the revision improves actual accountability. Version changes should be visible where prior outputs remain in use, with an appropriate path to contest or correct old determinations. Neither attachment to the original format nor wholesale abandonment is a sufficient response. The criterion is whether the revised instrument better supports its underlying purpose without imposing disproportionate burden.

##### HG.SB.05.02.H003 — Role and Money Shock Resilience

**Definition.**

Anticipate founder absence, lost or excess funding, review capture, unpopular decisions and compromised record continuity through explicit response paths


**Explanation.**

Institutional shocks test whether authority resides in replaceable functions or in particular people and funding relationships. The framework’s role-separation, money-flow and consequence discussions provide a way to inspect such dependencies. For each plausible shock, identify the decision holder, temporary operating limits, custody of essential records, authorized funding changes and independent review. Founder absence should not eliminate the ability to correct a claim; loss of a donor should not silently transfer control to a replacement; sudden surplus should not override precommitted purposes. An unpopular ruling should have a legitimate challenge route without making review subordinate to publicity. Scenarios are useful for locating single points of failure and defining transition responsibilities, but they are prospective tests. Claims of demonstrated resilience require evidence of actual controls or observed performance, not only a tabletop plan.

##### HG.SB.05.02.H004 — Mission Stability with Governed Method Change

**Definition.**

Protect the declared institutional purpose while allowing reviewable modification of procedures, funding routes or operators when conditions change


**Explanation.**

A stable mission does not require permanent procedures. The framework distinguishes the public trust claim from the arrangements that support it and allows instruments to be repaired when they drift. The relevant question is whether a proposed method change continues to discharge the original duty, or quietly changes who benefits, who decides, and what can be challenged. Identify the authority to amend a process, the reason for revision, the affected records and claims, and any required consultation or refusal rights. Preserve continuity through dated versions and a clear transition for people relying on earlier rules. Where the mission itself is being changed, describe that as a substantive governance decision rather than routine maintenance. Reviewable adaptation protects purpose without treating the founding design as infallible.

##### HG.SB.05.02.H005 — Consequence After Governance Failure

**Definition.**

Meaningful accountability alters authorization, records, money, access or service restoration rather than merely explaining why a failure occurred


A statement of regret is not a consequence unless decision rights, records, money, access or restoration change.

**Explanation.**

The framework states that a consequence path gives trust claims weight because failure must be answerable. An apology or explanation may communicate responsibility, but cannot substitute for a change in the affected arrangement. Depending on the breach, a response may narrow authorization, correct a public record, suspend status, reroute funds, restore access, require independent review or provide restitution. The consequence should be proportionate and documented, with an identified actor authorized to implement it. Distinguish the initial decision from evidence that the action was carried out; a promised correction may remain incomplete. Where restoration is appropriate, record the conditions and new status without pretending the failure never occurred. Accountability should protect affected people and make future reliance better grounded, rather than perform punishment for its own sake.

Related: HG.SB.02.01.G004
Related: HG.SB.03.01.A000

##### HG.SB.05.02.H006 — Public Function Without Incumbent

**Definition.**

A service remains answerable after the person who originated or operated it is replaced, rather than treating personal continuity as an institutional safeguard


**Explanation.**

A public function is not durable if only one incumbent knows its rules, holds its records or can authorize correction. The framework’s succession and role-separation material distinguishes originating contribution from continuing institutional authority. Inspect what happens when a founder, operator, trustee or reviewer leaves: who receives decision rights, how records transfer, which limits remain binding, and who can challenge the successor. A handoff should preserve public commitments and outstanding complaints while making any temporary service restriction explicit. Merely appointing a replacement is insufficient if passwords, funding control, interpretive authority or informal veto remain elsewhere. Conversely, acknowledging a founder's authorship need not confer permanent control. Replaceability is demonstrated through usable records, authorized transitions and operative review paths, not through a symbolic announcement of succession.


### Domain 05.03 — Public Records, Review and Correction
#### Family 05.03.A — Public Trust Surfaces, Disclosure and Decision-Point Legibility

This family examines how public trust claims reach people through marks, records, product interfaces and notices, and how those surfaces remain bounded by inspectable scope, evidence, status and correction.

**Shared family guidance.**
- Use the point at which reliance occurs to test whether a person can locate the claim’s scope, source, status and correction path. An attractive public presentation is not itself evidence of warranted reliance.

##### HG.SB.05.03.A000 — Public Trust Surfaces, Disclosure and Decision-Point Legibility

**Definition.**

A visible trust claim, badge, dashboard, page or notice should provide a usable route to its exact meaning, supporting structure, limits and correction path at the point of reliance. Legibility is proportionate and accessible, not a demand for faith or spectacular exposure.


**Explanation.**

The public surface is the encounter point between a system’s assertion and a person deciding whether to rely on it. The framework distinguishes the visible statement from the supporting arrangement of roles, evidence, records and consequences. A label such as reviewed or certified therefore needs a usable route to its object, method, authority, date, exclusions and challenge channel. The necessary information should be placed where reliance occurs, with additional detail accessible without making every user reconstruct an entire governance scheme. Disclosure must also respect privacy and avoid turning correction into public spectacle. The test is not whether a page looks official or comprehensive, but whether its presentation accurately bounds the decision a person can make. This describes a design and review criterion, not proof that any particular public claim has been validated.

Related: HG.SB.02.05.G003

##### HG.SB.05.03.A001 — Public Trust Surface

**Definition.**

A publicly encountered claim surface should connect its apparent meaning to inspectable criteria, scope, status, limits and channels for challenge. A visible claim should give an affected person a route from the surface to the scoped record, current status and correction channel; visibility without that route may leave reliance unsupported.


**Explanation.**

The framework identifies marks, registry entries, scores, governance pages, receipts and product workflow notices as public trust surfaces. Their common task is to translate a claim into an inspectable path rather than demand belief in the symbol. For example, a review badge should link to the precise review object, applicable criteria, reviewer role, date and limits; a public-benefit statement should connect to the rules that constrain resource and authority flows. A surface can be visually clear yet structurally misleading if the underlying record is absent, obsolete or inaccessible. Review both what the surface says and what a user can actually reach from it. The surface is neither an independent certification nor a substitute for corrective authority: its reliability depends on continuing alignment with the supporting system.

##### HG.SB.05.03.A002 — Surface as Doorway

**Definition.**

A visible mark or entry is an invitation to inspect the underlying review and record, not a self-validating reason to rely.


The doorway is the route from visible symbol to underlying record; it is not a second source of authority.

**Explanation.**

The doorway metaphor distinguishes presentation from substantiation. A certification mark is the entrance to criteria, scope, evidence, decision role, date, current status and consequence; a registry label is the entrance to its record and correction rules. The practical question is whether a person can follow that route without encountering an unsupported leap from symbol to endorsement. A decorative seal with no accessible review record is not strengthened by greater prominence. Conversely, a modest statement linked to a narrow and current review may support appropriately limited reliance. The doorway should also work in reverse: when a status changes, the visible claim must change with it. This is an interface and accountability relation, not a new institutional power conferred by the mark.

Related: HG.SB.02.03.A003

##### HG.SB.05.03.A003 — Decision-Point Legibility

**Definition.**

Put the relevant scope, authority, time and correction information where a person actually decides whether to rely, proportionate to the stakes.


Decision-point placement is a timing and usability requirement, distinct from making a record available somewhere else.

**Explanation.**

The framework observes that users encounter trust in actual workflows rather than only in governance documents. A disclosure placed in an archive may technically exist while failing to inform the person who is about to share data, accept a recommendation, purchase a service or rely on a status. Decision-point legibility asks what must be visible at that moment: the claim’s meaning, relevant limits, whether it is current, and how to challenge or exit. Higher-stakes decisions may require more prominent qualifications and stronger confirmation, while routine tasks should not be buried under exhaustive procedural text. The underlying detail can remain linked and inspectable. Evaluate legibility by following the user’s path and checking whether the information arrives before reliance, not merely by verifying that it appears somewhere on the website.

##### HG.SB.05.03.A004 — Visibility Without Spectacle

**Definition.**

Support reliance and correction through accessible records without public humiliation, inflated dashboards or indiscriminate exposure.


Proportionate disclosure avoids public humiliation without suppressing necessary grounds for challenge.

**Explanation.**

Visibility is useful when it makes claims, decisions and corrections answerable. It becomes spectacle when exposure itself is treated as the remedy or when status displays invite public judgment without adequate context. The framework explicitly distinguishes publicity from trust and recognizes that records need privacy boundaries. A proportionate public explanation may disclose the reviewed object, criteria, decision, date, status and route to contestation while restricting personal details or sensitive deliberation. Correction should update the operative record and the affected person’s options, not simply generate a more dramatic public statement. Review whether a disclosure is necessary for bounded reliance and challenge, whether it exposes more than that purpose requires, and whether it creates an actionable path. Less exposure is not automatically concealment; more exposure is not automatically accountability.

##### HG.SB.05.03.A005 — Public Trust Disclosure Questions

**Definition.**

Explain exactly what is claimed, what supports it, what is excluded, and what changes after error or correction.


**Explanation.**

A disclosure review can be organized around four questions. First, what proposition is being offered for reliance, and to which object, version and period does it apply? Second, what criteria, records and authorized decisions support that proposition? Third, what remains outside the review, including uncertainty, excluded uses and unresolved disputes? Fourth, if the claim proves wrong or becomes stale, who can revise status, correct the record and restore affected options? The framework’s examples of reviewed, certified, independent and non-extractive claims show why the same public word can conceal different scopes. Answering the questions makes the claim narrower but more usable. A completed disclosure checklist does not itself establish that the underlying evidence is sound or that the described correction mechanism functions.

##### HG.SB.05.03.A006 — Trust-Surface Maintenance

**Definition.**

Keep dates, links, scope and status synchronized with the actual decision and update process, so the interface does not lag behind reality.


Maintenance is a continuing synchronization duty; initial accuracy does not prevent later drift.

**Explanation.**

A public trust surface is a live representation of a governed record. It can become misleading without any initial falsehood: review scope changes, an authorization expires, a link breaks, an appeal succeeds or an operator revises the underlying standard. The framework connects public status to records, corrections and consequences, so maintenance requires clear responsibility for propagating those changes to each visible claim. Specify the source of truth, update authority, version and date fields, expiry or review triggers, and a route for reporting discrepancies. A stale badge or cached status should not silently continue to imply current approval. Maintenance also includes removing or qualifying claims that can no longer be supported. The existence of an update policy is only a proposed control until synchronization is checked in practice.

Related: HG.SB.01.01.A004
Related: HG.SB.02.06.B005

##### HG.SB.05.03.A007 — Public Legibility Versus Persuasion

**Definition.**

Ease of reading or attractive visuals cannot substitute for accurate scope and the ability to check, correct and refuse a claim.


**Explanation.**

Persuasion seeks assent; public legibility enables a person to decide what, if anything, to rely on. The framework warns that branding, dashboards, seals and institutional posture can imitate accountability while obscuring the underlying mechanism. Clear typography and accessible language are valuable, but they do not cure a missing record, exaggerated scope, unreviewable authority or ineffective appeal. Test a surface by asking whether a skeptical user can identify the precise claim, inspect its basis, understand exclusions and decline or challenge reliance without unreasonable burden. A visually modest notice with these properties may serve trust better than an impressive but unqualified endorsement. This distinction does not reject communication design; it places communication in service of accurate, bounded judgment rather than using aesthetic confidence as evidence.

Related: HG.SB.02.06.G005
#### Family 05.03.B — Registry, Receipts, Identity and Institutional Memory

This family develops the relation between inspectable institutional memory, precisely scoped identity, versioned receipts, record custody, correction, and privacy. The record supports a trust claim only to the extent that its evidence, authority and maintenance actually support it.

**Shared family guidance.**
- Inspect object identity, version, record custody, amendment history and access permissions. A stored receipt proves only what its recorded scope supports; neither storage nor public visibility guarantees truth or an effective remedy.

##### HG.SB.05.03.B000 — Registry, Receipts, Identity and Institutional Memory

**Definition.**

A maintained shared record preserves what object and version was evaluated, the supporting evidence, decision authority, scope, historical changes, privacy boundary and corrective responsibility. An inspectable registry coordinates knowledge without requiring agreement or permanent public exposure.


**Explanation.**

A registry is the institutional memory of a bounded trust claim, not a substitute for its underlying decision. Its entry must connect an identifiable object and version to the review performed, deciding authority, reasons, time, exclusions and present status. Subsequent amendments should leave an interpretable history, including corrections and retirement. That history lets different parties coordinate around a common record even while disputing its conclusions. The registry also requires a custodian, update permissions and a reachable correction route; otherwise it may preserve an obsolete or unilateral assertion. The framework distinguishes information needed for public inspection from protected audit material and information that should never be collected. The design question is therefore not how much can be displayed, but what trace supports accountable reliance without imposing unnecessary exposure.

Related: HG.SB.02.03.C005

##### HG.SB.05.03.B001 — Public Registry as Reality Layer

**Definition.**

A versioned, updated shared register makes claims, decision bases and status changes inspectable instead of privately rewritten or remembered only by an operator. The record must have bounded update authority and a correction path; a populated database alone is not proof that entries are current or contestable.


**Explanation.**

A public registry acts as a reality layer when a visible claim can be checked against a maintained record rather than accepted on the strength of a badge or operator statement. The framework identifies scope, criteria, current status, expiration, suspension and restoration as material elements. An entry should distinguish the thing reviewed from the organization displaying the result, and a change in product or criteria should trigger reconsideration of its applicability. The register is not automatically trustworthy: a directory without review grounds, an uncorrectable entry or a stale status can intensify false confidence. A responsible design assigns update and dispute authority, preserves relevant history, and provides enough public information to test the specific claim. Whether those processes function is an operational question beyond the presence of a database.

##### HG.SB.05.03.B002 — Common Knowledge Engine

**Definition.**

Shared reasons, status and records enable informed coordination and disagreement without requiring unanimous belief or exposing every private deliberation.


**Explanation.**

Common knowledge in this setting is an accessible reference structure, not a requirement that participants reach the same conclusion. A dated record of what was claimed, what was considered and what was decided allows a user, reviewer and operator to discuss the same object without relying on private recollection. The record can include uncertainty, contested interpretations and status changes; disagreement remains possible because reasons and boundaries are explicit. This function also depends on access design. Sensitive care details, security material and confidential deliberation need not become public for the decision basis to be inspectable through suitable channels.
